full_text:
Attached is IFPI's input to the European Commission's inception impact assessment on Digital Services Act: deepening the Internal Market and clarifying responsibilities for digital services.

How the Digital Services Act (DSA) Can Help Foster a More Responsible Online Environment June 2020 ABOUT IFPI IFPI represents the interests of the recording industry worldwide. We have some 1,300 members around the world and in all major European markets, ranging from small-tomedium enterprise (SME) to global labels. We work to promote the value of recorded music, to campaign for the rights of record producers and to expand the commercial uses of recorded music in all markets where our members operate. THE ISSUE1 In its announcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) framework, the European Commission recognizes the need for a safer internet teeming with legal content, and greater accountability of digital services, including and in particular online intermediaries, to help achieve that. We strongly agree. Host providers, access providers, domain registrars and registries, app stores and search engines, for example, are all gatekeepers to or support the distribution of content and should have adequate responsibilities and obligations ("duties of care") that are essential to tackling illegal content online. They can do better. In recent years, technology has advanced by leaps and bounds, enabling the accomplishment of tasks that would have been unimaginable when the current laws were written. Today, many of these companies are among the world's most sophisticated and innovative, and well-positioned to stop and prevent the distribution of illegal content. If they fail to fulfill their r esponsibilities, the risks are significant - the European cultural sectors' eco-system (in particular when it comes to the creation of new European content) could be harmed, and European economic growth and digital innovation hampered. Europe has made grea t efforts to update and harmonise copyright across the European Union. However, the measures and procedures to enforce those rights online have not been updated and harmonised. An essential feature of fair and effective online enforcement of rights is the adoption of robust responsibilities and

1 This position paper addresses the key elements of the part of the Commission's Digital Services Act package concerning responsibilities and obligations of digital services. It does not address issues dealing with potential ex ante rules applicable to large online platforms acting as gatekeepers, or competition aspects.

obligations for digital services, including online intermediaries. Until that is achieved, the European digital market will not perform to its full potential. A well-functioning internal market of intellectual prop erty rights enforcement is key to achieving a level playing field among all businesses, increasing consumers' trust in the digital marketplace and ensuring legal certainty, transparency and a healthy ecosystem where all its participants are fairly rewarded. THE CONTEXT The music industry was one of the first to respond to the digital challenge. Prior to returning to growth in 2015, the industry experienced more than 15 years of significant revenue decline mostly due to large-scale unauthorised use of music online which continues to affect the creative industry. Throughout that difficult period, record companies continued their investments in artists, global systems and infrastructure, which has enabled them to license more than 60 million tracks to hundreds of digital services across Europe. Consequently, music fans today enjoy access to unprecedented amounts of diverse European music, and European artists have access to global markets and the opportunity to connect with fans across the world. However, unauthorised use of music online remains an industrial-scale problem for the recording industry. IFPI, its National Groups and member record labels send out millions of takedown notices to online services every year which requires a huge human effort and significant financial resources. However, the vast majority of these notices refer to content that has already been notified to the same online service before - in 2018 this was the case for 88 per cent of notices sent by IFPI. This data shows the ineffectiveness of the current system. As a result, the enormous potential of European music continues to be hampered. On the one hand, illegal services making money on the back of unauthorised online distribution of music can establish themselve s almost anywhere, while providing copyright infringing content, across borders and simultaneously in any number of territories. Yet, when trying to stop the operations of these illegal businesses ‒ whether by taking direct actions against infringers or by seeking injunctions against intermediary services used by the infringers ‒ right holders need to pursue legal actions Member State by Member State. This makes addressing online infringements in the EU slow and expensive and limits the effectiveness of any actions by right holders to protect their rights. On the other hand, illegal services now typically use and rely on a number of different digital services including online intermediaries, such as: internet access providers;

hosting service providers; Con tent Delivery Networks (CDNs); search engines; payment providers; domain registrars; app store operators; etc. There is a need to provide for different and truly effective measures and procedures to ensure those digital services play their part in reducing unauthorised uses. In concrete terms this means, for instance, introducing an obligation to ensure accuracy of data that digital services keep about their customers. To date, it is often not possible to pursue direct action against illegal websites becau se the operators act in complete anonymity, protected by shell companies or domain name privacy services, or both, and the digital services and intermediaries used by these illegal websites do not require their customers to provide proof of their true identity and contact details. The Commission has acknowledged that there is a problem with online enforcement of rights in Europe, and that more should be done to strengthen the current EU enforcement system. 2 So far, the Commission has chosen only non-legislative instruments to tackle the problem (e.g. the 2017 Guidelines on the Enforcement Directive). However, those instruments or voluntary enforcement measures are not sufficient to remedy the problems the recording industry is facing. HOW CAN THE DSA HELP? The DSA framework should include instruments which enhance the accountability of all types of digital services and update their responsibilities and obligations to tackle illegal content online, including copyright infringements, more effectively. We note that this can, and should be achieved by complementing the E-Commerce Directive without opening it:
• "Duty of Care": All digital services, which are being used to infringe copyrights, should be obliged to take reasonable steps to stop, limit and prevent infringements ("duty of care"). The content of those responsibilities and obligations and which steps the digital services including online intermediary service can be reasonably expected to take should depend on the types of services, but all services including smaller ones should be covered. The duty of care should, for instance, include the obligation to stop providing services to illegal websites, and to implement an effective "repeat infringer" policy.

• "Notice and Stay Down" obligation for passive host ing providers: Online hosting services of a "mere technical, automatic and passive nature", eligible for liability "safe harbours", should ensure that illegal content that has been

2 In May 2015 by announcing its Digital Single Market (DSM) Strategy the Commission said that it would make legislative proposals in 2016 "modernising enforcement of intellectual property rights, focusing on commercial-scale infringements (the 'follow the money' approach) as well as its cross - border applicability".

removed does not reappear on their services. We do not however see the need to further regulate the procedural rules regarding notice and take down, such as the form of notices or timeframes for take downs, for the removal of content. They work generally well in the case of our industry, providing flexibility for the different types of services and content.

• Improved Transparency Obligations: The transparency requirements under the current EU legislation should be improved, notably by requiring digital services to implement effective Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) policies and by introducing an explicit legal basis for a public WHOIS registry which should, at a very minimum, contain all data already required to be made publicly available under existing law (Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive), as well as such other information that is necessary for right holders to pursue legal actions to protect their copyrights.

• Adjusting Copyright Enforcement Measures to the Digital Single Market: Furthermore, because copyright infringements are borderless, the DSA should help right holders in protecting their rights effectively across the EU; without the need to bring actions in each individual Member State against the same infringers, the same content, and the same infringing activity, be it in relation to infringing services directly or against digital services including online intermediaries.

• Complement Responsibilities and Obligations without changing the scope of, and eligibility for, "safe harbours": The definitions and the types of activities and online intermediary se rvices eligible for the safe harbours should remain unchanged. The EU acquis should be consolidated. In particular, the current distinction used in the E-Commerce Directive between "active" and "passive" online intermediaries should not be changed by the D SA to avoid altering the careful balance in the E-Commerce Directive between the need to protect content owners and the need to enable the development of the Internet. For instance, re-defining the criteria for an "active" intermediary in a narrower manner in the DSA, could extend safe harbour privileges to services that were not meant to be entitled to them under the E-Commerce Directive. Amending the scope of the safe harbours would undermine the EU and national jurisprudence (e.g. CJEU decision in L'Oréal v eBay, Google France 3) and the recent legislative developments (e.g. the DSM Directive4), which have helpfully clarified the eligibility criteria for safe harbour protection. The DSA should not

3 C-324/09 - L'Oréal and Others; C-236/08 - Google France and Google. 4 Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market.

weaken those criteria but complement and strengthen the responsibilities and obligations of digital services operating in the digital markets. We detail our comments on the above-mentioned elements further in this paper.
1. MORE ROBUST RESPONSIBILITIES AND OBLIGATIONS FOR DIGITAL SERVICES, INCLUDING ONLINE INTERMEDIARIES ("DUTY OF CARE")

A. DIGITAL SERVICES, INCLUDING ONLINE INTERMEDIARIES MUST DO MORE The Issue: Illegal online services use and rely on a variety of digital services, including internet access providers, hosting service providers, Content Delivery Network (CDN) providers, search engines, payment providers, domain registrars, app store operators, operating systems and web browsers, among others. There have been some examples of voluntary cooperation between right holders and intermediaries or other digital services.5 However, such voluntary agreements are no substitutes for a robust legal framework, setting out clear responsibilities and obligations. Experience shows that voluntary agreements are more likely to be negotiated and work, where they provide for a way for digital services to comply with their statutory obligations. The Proposed Solution: EU legislation should establish obligations on all digital services including online intermediaries to take reasonable steps to stop and prevent online copyright infringements. The responsibilities and obligations should apply broadly and should extend t o all digital services, including online intermediaries, providing services to businesses or consumers residing in the EU. The nature of the obligations and responsibilities, the triggering factors and which steps the online intermediary can be reasonably expected to take, depends on the circumstances and the types of services offered. They should, for example, include an obligation to implement an effective "repeat infringer policy" to avoid that the same account holder or website operator can

5 For example, there are Memorandums of Understanding or Code of Conducts in place in some countries between the advertising industry and right holders, or, in Denmark and Portugal, voluntary agreements between right holders and internet access providers complem ent existing court and administrative procedures.

continue t o infringe copyright in spite of the fact that the service provider knows or is aware of the account to be found to be infringing, e.g. following a notice from the right holders. Thus, once the service provider knows or is aware of repeat infringements com ing from the same account or customer, effective actions need to be taken, e.g. temporary suspension of accounts. Digital services should also stop enabling or facilitating the operation of illegal websites by providing them services or means to operate. Once a digital service has actual knowledge, or has become aware of facts or circumstances of which it becomes apparent, that a website to which it provides services infringes intellectual property rights, it should cease providing services to that website for as long as the illegal activity continues. This may require digital services to undertake reasonable checks to investigate the nature of their customers' business to ensure that unauthorised activities are not being supported. For example, if a webs ite owner wishes to register a website, the name of which raises clear red flags (e.g. www.leakedmusicfor free.com), the domain register should inquire with the registrant about the purpose of the website. Similarly, given that online piracy occurs very of ten via mobile devices involving mobile apps, app store operators should take a more proactive approach and remove apps which facilitate online copyright infringements. There are also a number of measures that app store operators can take to prevent that such apps appear on their platforms in the first place, e.g. by implementing an effective repeat infringer policy and take action in case of "red flags" e.g. if a name of an app relates to a known pirate site. The responsibilities and obligations should, in principle, apply regardless of the size of the digital service. Small and medium sized companies could do as much harm as the large ones. For example, some of the online intermediaries that are used by illegal services are relatively small and sometimes working in cahoots with other smaller facilitators of illegal activities. If the duty of care would exclude such small and medium sized companies, it would not achieve its objective to assist right holders in tackling illegal content online. Non-compliance with those obligations and responsibilities should result in meaningful sanctions.
B. PASSIVE HOSTING SERVICE PROVIDERS MUST ENSURE "NOTICE AND STAY DOWN" The Issue:

The current "Notice and Takedown" requirement is an ineffective tool to address the shee r volume of copyright infringing content online. Service providers often remove only the individual URL named in the notice - instead of removing all the infringing copies of the same sound recording - from their services and do nothing to ensure that infr inging copies are not immediately re-uploaded. According to IFPI data for 2018, 88 per cent of the IFPI notices refer to content that has already been notified to the same online service before For example, Lady Gaga's "Born this way" was notified to cybe rlocker Rapidgator 4,805 times after the first notice. The Beatles' "Let it be" was notified to Rapidgator 9,100 times following the first notice. And, in spite of all these thousands of notices, these recordings continue to re-appear on a regular basis on the same site. The Proposed Solution: EU legislation should clarify that upon becoming aware of an infringement a hosting service provider must (i) remove all copies of the same work/sound recording; and (ii) ensure the same work or recording (or a c opy thereof) is not re-posted or uploaded in the future (i.e. "stay down" obligation). At both the EU and Member State levels, the respective competent courts have firmly established a "Stay Down" obligation.6 A "Stay Down" obligation is consistent with Article 15 of the E-Commerce Directive. Ensuring "stay down" only requires certain measures and action in relation to specific content.7 For passive host providers that comply with the notice and stay down obligation, the EU legislator could consider th e introduction of a so-called "Good Samaritan" clause, to ensure that these services can still enjoy protection under the existing safe harbour regime.
C. TRANSPARENCY

6 At EU level, two important CJEU decisions support a "stay down" obligation: CJEU C-324/09 - L'Oreal vs Ebay; CJEU C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek vs Facebook. There have also been a number of decisions from German courts (Federal Court of Justice ("FCJ"), 15 August 2013, No. I ZR 80/12 - Rapidshare; Higher Regional Court of Hamburg, 1 July 2015, No. 5 U 87/12 - GEMA vs YouTube; Regional Court of Hamburg, 12 June 2018, No. 308 O 224/18 - GEMA vs. Rapidgator) and from courts in Italy (e.g. Supreme Court 18 March 2019, No. 9133/2015 - RTI v Yahoo; Court of Turin, 24 January 2018, No. 342/2018 Delta TV vs. Dailymotion). 7 This position was essentially confirmed by the CJEU in a case against Facebook - CJEU C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek vs Facebook.

The Issue: In the physical world "Know Your Business Customer" processes are already applied in a number of sectors, such as in the financial and legal services sectors, to fight money laundering and other forms of financial crime by ensuring that the identities of new clients are verified and accurate client data are being held by the service providers. In the EU, such obligations were already introduced for many sectors since the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive in 2005. 8 Equally, corporate entities are required to disclose their accurate legal address es and identities of responsible individuals, which is essential in enforcing the law and holding them accountable. Similarly, application of KY BC rules to digital services would make it harder for dodgy companies and entrepreneurs to operate online, without regard to copyright, consumer protection, tax, and other applicable legislation. The lack of transparency online and the ease with which operators of unauthorised services can hide their identities, is one of the most important hurdles for right holders to protect their rights. Currently, operators can act in complete anonymity, protected by domain privacy services or shell companies, while digital services often fail to require that their customers provide proof of their true identities and correct co ntact details. This seriously undermines online enforcement efforts, including attempts to contact or bring actions against the suspected infringers. The Proposed Solutions: To improve transparency, the DSA should include the following elements:
I. "KNOW YOUR BUSINESS CUSTOMER" POLICIES Legislation should require that digital services including online intermediaries implement effective Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) policies, i.e. intermediaries need to ensure they verify the identity of their business customers and have accurate and meaningful information about their customers. At a minimum, such information should include the information that services are required to provide under Article 5 of the E-Commerce

8 See Directive 2005/60/EC of 26 October 2005 on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing. The relevant "Know your customer" obligations have been implemented across the EU, e.g.: Art. 29 of the UK Regulation of 2017 on Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds; section 11 et seq. of the German Money Laundering Act.

Directive, e.g. the true and verified n ame, physical address, email address and telephone number of their customers. In case of legal entities, the information should also include up-to-date information of the company directors or other responsible persons. Depending on the type of service, it could also include bank account details. In addition to the initial verification of the details provided, digital services should apply regular checks to ensure that the details remain accurate and up to date. This obligation should also apply to any reseller of the original digital service. There should be sanctions for the failure to comply with the obligation. Further, digital services should terminate services to websites or online services where the information these services have provided turns out to be incorrect (regardless of the KYBC process followed), or where the services do not comply with the transparency obligations, e.g. if a website does not publish information required under Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive (see below). II. BETTER ENFORCEMENT OF NON-COMPLIANCE WITH ARTICLE 5 OF THE E-COMMERCE DIRECTIVE EU legislation on transparency should be complemented by better enforcement of non-compliance with Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive at national level. Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive requires all EU-based service p roviders to "render easily, directly and permanently accessible to" EU consumers and authorities at least the name, geographical address, e-mail address and other information depending on the business model. In IFPI's experience this obligation is rarely being complied with, in particular by illegal services. There are a number of reasons for this, including that in most Member States there is no effective enforcement and no deterrent consequences when a service is found to be in breach of this obligation. Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive should therefore be complemented to ensure that it applies to all services that are being provided to EU citizens, regardless of the physical location of the business, and there should be deterrent sanctions in case o f non - compliance. In addition, digital services should not provide services to websites that do not comply with Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive (see above).

III. LEGAL BASIS FOR A PUBLIC REGISTER ABOUT DOMAIN REGISTRANTS Following GDPR coming into force, the Internet Cooperation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) 9 introduced a Temporary Specification for WHOIS requiring registrars and registries to redact the vast majority of WHOIS data pertaining to European domain registrants (irrespective of whet her they are natural or legal persons). The result has been an almost total withdrawal of the public WHOIS register which has significantly impacted our ability to obtain data necessary for our enforcement and litigation actions. Discussions are ongoing at ICANN to develop an "access model" but there is a lack of confidence amongst stakeholders about this process and the prospects of it arriving at a workable solution. Legislative intervention is needed urgently to clarify the public interest in a public W HOIS registry. Therefore, the EU should introduce an explicit legal basis for a public WHOIS registry which should, at a minimum, contain all data already required to be made publicly available under Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive.
2. EFFECTIVE TOOLS FOR ONLINE ENFORCEMENT OF COPYRIGHTS

A. EFFECTIVE INJUNCTIVE RELIEF The Issue: Injunctive relief is a key remedy for right holders, but the effectiveness of the remedy is currently undermined in many Member States because, while unauthorised websites operate indiscriminately across Europe, right holders have to take action country by country based on each Member State's legal system. This is slow and prohibitively costly for most right holders. Furthermore, most European legal systems do not allow right holders to seek "dynamic" or "catalogue wide" injunctions making it unreasonably difficult for right holders to effectively protect their rights across Europe. The Proposed Solutions: Positive obligations and responsibilities under the DSA should be coupled with meaningful enforcement measures, including injunctions against all types of

9 ICANN is a multi-stakeholder group that coordinates several databases relating to the internet.

digital services to stop or prevent infringements. Further, EU legislation should address the lack of a cross-border effect of enforcement measures, and, regarding injunctive relief, should ensure that such injunctions are effective and sustainable in dealing with unauthorised services.
I. CROSS-BORDER EFFECT OF INJUNCTIONS The most compelling example to stress the importance of "cross - border" injunctions is the notorious BitTorrent site "The Pirate Bay". The operators of The Pirate Bay have been subject to civil and criminal litigation in Sweden, and to criminal actions in Belgium and Finland. The cases were successful, and appeals were rejected by all instances including by the European Court of Human Rights. Actions against intermediaries, e.g. to block access to the site, have been successful in 20 countries around the world including 13 EU Member States. The CJEU has also confirmed the operators of the website s are engaged in copyright restricted acts. However, in spite of these multiple actions, the site remains online and accessible in many EU countries. The DSA could improve the situation for right holders by introducing measures which could help to ensure cross-border effect of certain protective and preventive measures: (1) If the defendant operates in multiple EU Member States (either because the defendant is the operator of an unauthorised website, which is accessible throughout the EU, or because it provides services across a number of Member States), national courts should be empowered by EU legislation to award damages and issue injunctions with respect to all the affected Member States, without right holders being required to provide extensive evidence or legal arguments regarding all the different EU jurisdictions. Such crossborder effect is justified because the high level of harmonisation of EU copyright law and civil enforcement measures and procedures; an infringement in one country will also constitute a copyright infringement in other EU Member States, and the inf ringement would be subject to the same or similar civil enforcement measures and procedures.

(2) In case of applications for "no fault" third party injunctions (available under applicable EU law) related to the same unauthorised service but different national respondent intermediaries, EU legislation should empower Member States to

introduce expedited procedures to ensure that the same category of online intermediaries will take the same measures in relation to the same infringing service. This could occur within a national court process where judgements from other EU Member States are used as the bas is for granting similar injunctions. 10 The same results could also be achieved through administrative procedures involving competent agencies ordering the relevant intermediaries to take such measures in their respective countries. Finally, the DSA could also play an important role in encouraging and promoting cross-industry agreements to facilitate voluntary implementation by intermediaries of judgements from other EU Member States, which could be prompted by the enhanced cooperation among public authorities in Member States. II. DYNAMIC AND CATALOGUE-WIDE INJUNCTIONS Right holders need to have recourse to measures that:
a. are sufficiently flexible to remain effective over time, i.e. injunctions or other measures that cover the provision of an infringing online service without being limited to specific online locations (URL addresses) as these are easy to change; and

b. cover the right holder's entire catalogue (the infringer is enjoined from infringing works or recordings owned or controlled by the plaintiff/ applicant); and

c. are genuinely available on an expedited basis where the circumstances require.

10 For example, if right holders were successful in obtaining a judgement against French ISPs requiring them to block access to The Pirate Bay, a German court should grant a similar order for German r ight holders against the same site in relation to German ISPs without the need to litigate the issue whether the underlying service is infringing.

Free Knowledge Advocacy Group EU welcome the debate on the responsibilities of digital services. We believe that a regulatory framework must preserve and promote the freedom of imparting and receiving information without interference by public authority; promote freedom of expression; and protect users from harmful and illegal activities. 

For all measures contemplated at the EU level, including legislative action, non-binding ones, and voluntary cooperation, careful consideration needs to be given to how changes in the incentive structure might affect the enjoyment of fundamental rights. As the roadmap states, “protections of users’ rights - including the freedom to receive or impart information - are not always sufficiently robust across the board.” 

Special consideration needs to be given to how the commercialization of the public debate (which now takes place on platforms regulated by private terms of service) affects the freedom of expression. New regulatory instruments must not create incentives for overblocking content. For this reason, we strongly believe that the foundation of the e-Commerce Directive (liability exemption for intermediaries and no general monitoring obligation) should remain in place.

As stated in the roadmap, an important step in this direction would be to reduce information asymmetries between platforms and users by improving transparency around online advertising and algorithmic accountability. Users of digital services should always be able to tell the difference between user-generated content and paid content. Moreover, users must have an accessible option to sort the content displayed to them. It is clear that some of these problems, including issues related to the spread of misinformation, are inextricably linked to the data-driven business model of social media platforms. Introducing interoperability requirements could enable users to choose different services based on different business models.

The Free Knowledge Advocacy Group EU unites the European Wikimedia chapters and communities so they can have a clear and coherent position on major legislative and political changes affecting the vision, mission and values of the Wikimedia movement. We support the feedback of the Wikimedia Foundation on the topic.

The Motion Picture Association (MPA) welcomes this opportunity to comment on the combined evaluation roadmap/inception impact assessment.
 
MPA members are leading producers and distributors of diverse film, series, television and online content enjoyed by European audiences via lawful digital services. MPA members are also leaders in fighting against illegal and harmful content online, both through the exercise of their own editorial responsibility, and through their extensive use of the tools available under the E-Commerce Directive (ECD) as well as other EU and national legal instruments.
 
We recall that a central goal of the Commission’s intended proposal for a new Digital Services Act is to lay down “more stringent” rules for the responsibilities of digital services. This overall goal needs to be borne in mind when considering all policy options, especially where the Commission considers updating and modernising the ECD. Any such exercise should in no event lead to broader safe harbours and fewer responsibilities, or less potential liability, for digital services.  
 
With these considerations in mind, we invite the European Commission to consider the following recommendations for the DSA:
 
- Embrace a “per-problem” approach: Instead of a horizontal harmonisation of core liability rules, the Commission should embrace a more targeted “per problem” approach via the creation of new specific obligations for service providers that would be complementary to the well-functioning framework already provided by the ECD.

- Uphold the E-Commerce Directive: The ECD’s framework, which has been clarified and updated with case law from the European Court of Justice, remains fundamentally valid today, and we support the Commission’s plan to uphold its structure while strengthening and upgrading the liability regime to make the internet a safer place for citizens and businesses operating in it.
 
- Remain faithful to the objective of “upgrading” liabilities and responsibilities through “more stringent” rules: MPA supports the Commission’s overall goal to lay down “more stringent” rules for the responsibilities of digital services, as well as its goal of taking the existing framework and upgrading the liabilities and responsibilities of digital intermediation services whilst not detracting from the existing liability regime.
 
- No erosion of Articles 12-15 ECD: We particularly urge the Commission to preserve and not weaken the existing EU law, embodied in Recital 42 of the ECD and the relevant CJEU case law, that defines the boundaries of Articles 12-15 ECD.
 
- No new liability shields for platforms: The Commission should be equally skeptical of active intermediaries seeking broad new liability shields and any assertion that they are somehow necessary “to remove disincentives for voluntary actions to address illegal content”.
 
- Use the DSA to introduce specific obligations for service providers: The targeted, “per-problem” approach described above should include the introduction of effective and carefully crafted obligations for service providers.
 
- These specific obligations should include a “know your business customer” (KYBC) obligation to deliver on the unfulfilled promise of Article 5 ECD and create a safer online business environment.
 
- Use the DSA to clarify access to WHOIS data:  Access to WHOIS data is essential in combatting illegal and harmful content online. We urge the Commission to apply such schemes not only to commercial users of marketplaces, as initially set out, but also to business customers of other key services.
 
- Use the DSA to introduce rules for staydown, repeat offenders, and trusted flaggers, but do not pursue a “one-size-fits-all” approach: A horizontal approach would be unworkable, as it would necessarily have to be founded on the lowest common denominators and would therefore weaken the current system as established in targeted legal instruments and case law.
 
Please find further details attached.

Any such exercise should in no event lead to broader safe harbours and fewer responsibilities, or less potential liability, for digital services.

With these considerations in mind, we invite the European Commission to consider the following recommendations for the DSA:

- Embrace a "per-problem" approach: Instead of a horizontal harmonisation of core liability rules, the Commission should embrace a more targeted "per problem" approach via the creation of new specific obligations for service providers that would be complementary to the well-functioning framework already provided by the ECD.

- Uphold the E-Commerce Directive: The ECD's framework, which has been clarified and updated with case law from the European Court of Justice, remains fundamentally valid today, and we support the Commission's plan to uphold its structure while strengthening and upgrading the liability regime to make the internet a safer place for citizens and businesses operating in it.

- Remain faithful to the objective of "upgrading" liabilities and responsibilities through "more stringent" rules: MPA supports the Commission's overall goal to lay down "more stringent" rules for the responsibilities of digital services, as well as its goal of taking the existing framework and upgrading the liabilities and responsibilities of digital intermediation services whilst not detracting from the existing liability regime.

- No erosion of Articles 12-15 ECD: We particularly urge the Commission to preserve and not weaken the existing EU law, embodied in Recital 42 of the ECD and the relevant CJEU case law, that defines the boundaries of Articles 12-15 ECD.

- No new liability shields for platforms: The Commission should be equally skeptical of active intermediaries seeking broad new liability shields and any assertion that they are somehow necessary "to remove disincentives for voluntary actions to address illegal content".

- Use the DSA to introduce specific obligations for service providers: The targeted, "per-problem" approach described above should include the introduction of effective and carefully crafted obligations for service providers.

- These specific obligations should include a "know your business customer" (KYBC) obligation to deliver on the unfulfilled promise of Article 5 ECD and create a safer online business environment.

- Use the DSA to clarify access to WHOIS data: Access to WHOIS data is essential in combatting illegal and harmful content online. We urge the Commission to apply such schemes not only to commercial users of marketplaces, as initially set out, but also to business customers of other key services.

- Use the DSA to introduce rules for staydown, repeat offenders, and trusted flaggers, but do not pursue a "one-size-fits-all" approach: A horizontal approach would be unworkable, as it would necessarily have to be founded on the lowest common denominators and would therefore weaken the current system as established in targeted legal instruments and case law.

Motion Picture Association (MPA) comments on the combined evaluation roadmap/inception impact assessment

"Digital Services Act package: deepening the Internal Market and clarifying responsibilities for digital services"

The Motion Picture Association (MPA) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the combined evaluation roadmap/inception impact assessment "Digital Services Act package: deepening the Internal Market and clarifying responsibilities for digital services".

This consultation is of key importance. MPA members are leading producers and distributors of diverse film, series, television and online content enjoyed by European audiences via lawful digital services. MPA members are also leaders in fighting against illegal and harmful content online, both through the exercise of their own editorial responsibility, and through their extensive us e of the tools available under the E - Commerce Directive (ECD) as well as other EU and national legal instruments.

We recall that a central goal of the Commission's intended proposal for a new Digital Services Act is to lay down "more stringent" rules for the responsibilities of digital services. This overall goal needs to be borne in mind when considering all policy options, especially where the Commission considers updating and modernising the ECD. Any s uch exercise should in no event lead to broader safe ha rbours and fewer responsibilities, or less potential liability, for digital services.

With these con siderations in mind, we invite the European Commission to consider the following recommendations for the DSA:

• Embrace a "per-problem" approach. The MPA considers that, instead of a horizontal harmonisation of core liability rules, the Commission should embrace a more targeted "per problem" approach via the creation of new specific obligations for service providers that would be complementary to the well-functioning framework already provided by the ECD. These should include inter alia the introduction of effective and comprehensive "know your business customer" schemes for digital services.

MOTION PICTURE ASSOCIATION EMEA

• Uphold the E-Commerce Directive. The ECD is built upon three pillars: the country of origin principle, a ban on the imposition of general monitoring obligations on passive service providers and specific limitations on potential liability. This framework, which has been subsequently clarified and updated with case law from the European Court of Justice, remains fundamentally valid today, and we sup port the Commission's plan to uphold this structure while strengthening and upgrading the liability regime to make the internet a safer place for citizens and businesses operating in it.

• Remain faithful to the objective of "upgrading" liabilities and responsibilities through "more stringent" rules. MPA supports the Commission's overall goal to lay down "more stringent" rules for the responsibilities of digital services, as well as its goal of taking the existing framework and upgrading the liabilities and responsibilities of digital intermediation services whilst not detracting from the existing liability regime. As the Commission is considering "harmonised notice-andaction systems", "clarifying liability rules" and "removing disincentives for voluntary actions to address illegal content", the Commission must take care that the expected positive indirect impacts for qua lity media and others engaged in legitimate trade are not offset by a net weakening or downgrading of digital services' responsibilities to address illegal content.
• No erosion of Articles 12-15 ECD. We particularly urge the Commission to preserve and not weaken the existing EU law, embodied in Recital 42 of the ECD and the relevant CJEU case law, that defines the boundaries of Articles 12-15 ECD. As set out in the Annex to this submission, the ECD has proven to be sufficiently flexible to deal with the em ergence of new services. The clear and essential distinction between active and passive services lies at the heart of this success. Those opposed to the distinction, which is now embedded in European jurisprudence, wish to: (a) avoid liability, and (b) advocate for further platform protections.
• No new liability shields for platforms. The Commission should be equally skeptical of active intermediaries seeking broad new liability shields and any assertion that they are someho w necessary "to remove disincentives for voluntary actions to address illegal content". MPA does not support the inclusion of new liability shield provisions in the DSA. Experience in the other jurisdictions has shown that such provision s complicate action against illegal services and ha ve given rise to extensive debate across the political spectrum. The Annex to this submission sets out more fully our concerns about the lack of evidence to support the importation of such measures, which would be fundamenta lly inconsistent with the objective of "upgrading" liability through "more stringent" rules.
• Use the DSA to introduce specific obligations for service providers. The targeted, "per-problem" approach described above should include the introduction of effec tive and carefully crafted obligations for service providers. These additional responsibilities should be consistent by platform type. This work does not preclude additional regulatory measures to address issues arising from systemic online intermediary services. Understanding that the objective of this exercise is to lay down "more stringent" rules of responsibility for online players, we believe that the existing framework would be strengthened by the introduction of specific obligations, not hindering the liability framework.

• These specific obligations should include a "know your business customer" (KYBC) obligation to deliver on the unfulfilled promise of Article 5 ECD and create a safer online business environment. As a global leader in the investigation of, and pursuit of legal remedies against illegal

services, the MPA struggles daily against an array of identity concealment tactics by illegal operators of services who ignore with impunity their basic obligations to identify themselves under Article 5 of the ECD. We urge the Commission to apply such schemes not only to commercial users of marketplaces, as initially set out, but also to business customers of other key services. Furthermore, d issuasive financial penalties should be introduced for non-compliance with the KYBC obligation. This would result in a real, tangible, complementary solution to at last fulfil the intent of Article 5 ECD for all illegal and harmful content, with minimal burdens on legitimate businesses. The Annex to this submission more fully describes MPA's views on this opportunity to strengthen the online ecosystem.

• Use the DSA to clarify access to WHOIS data. Access to WHOIS data is essential in combatting illegal and harmful content online. We believe that the DSA creates an opportunity for the Commission to provide additional clarification to eliminate misinterpretations that have unnecessarily hampered access to Internet domain registration data and confirm the need for access to WHOIS data as necessary for the public interest.

• Use the DSA to introduce rules for staydown, repeat offenders, and trusted flaggers, but do not pursue a "one-size-fits-all" approach. We urge the Commission to reject a "one size fits all" approach to notice and action rules/procedures which would address all types of illegal and harmful content on online intermediary services, from infringements of copyright to hate speech and terrorist content. A horizontal approach would be unworkable, as it would necessarily have to be founded on the lowest common denominators and would therefore weaken the current system as established in targeted legal instruments and case law. W hen considering targeted approaches to notice-and-action, the Commission needs to carefully consider the high-level objective of having less availability online of illegal (and harmful) goods, content and services and of avoiding burdensome processes that would ultimately lead to more illegal and harmful content being online or remaining available for a longer period of time. Any such targeted notice-andaction schemes should always include, as a minimum, the following elements, albeit implemented in a manner which delivers the above objectives for the specific content type: o an expeditious stay-down obligation for notified content (including for equivalent infringements); o mandatory repeat offender policies, including an obligation to make such policies publicly available; and, o fast-track procedures for trusted flaggers, including an obligation to publish all policies applicable to trusted flaggers.

Annex to MPA Submission: Legal and policy context for the "per problem approach"

1. The existing ECD liability privilege framework remains relevant and useful

The Commission rightfully identifies that there is today a wider spectrum of digital services than in 2000. These services, which intermediate content and whose activity is not of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature, include social media platforms, media-sharing platforms and search engines. These services have indeed been able to grow and flourish in Europe also thanks to the existing legislative framework. The concerns which have arisen typically relate to questions that should be treated in a manner that departs from the ECD, and that are often linked to services that are systemic in nature. But the arrival of new services does not diminish the continuing relevance of Articles 12 to 15 ECD. The activities of these new services are completely distinct from the services dealt with in Articles 12 to 15, and there is no reason to regulate them in the framework of the liability privileges in that instrument. Articles 12 to 15 cover p assive services, such as internet access providers and website infrastructure providers. Such services remain the backbone of the internet and play the most essential role in getting digital services to the end user. No digital service can be provided without internet access ("mere conduit" covered by Article 12 ECD), website infrastructure ("hosting providers" covered by Articl e 14 ECD), and improved content delivery through "caching" (covered by Article 13). Importantly, the ECD does not establish liability for digital services but instead only creates liability privileges for these limited digital services, and under very specific conditions.

• The ECD is explicit in Recital 42 that these exemptions from liability cover only cases where the activity of the information society service provider is limited to activity which i s of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature.

Limiting the liability of newer, non-passive services such as social media and media-sharing in the framework of a revised ECD would defeat the purpose of the DSA: It would diminish rather than enhance incentives to behave responsibly for powerful services. Many of these newer services have long tried to muddy the waters by claiming that they are "hosting providers" in the sense of Article 14 ECD and should therefore be conditionally exempted from liability. The same services advocate today for "clarifying" the scope of Article 14 (by ab olishing the distinction between active and passive platforms) and for introducing broader liability shields.

The distinction between passive and active is clear and essential As referred to above, in order for a hosting provider to benefit from the ECD liability privilege, the European Court of Justice (CJEU) has ruled, with reference to Recital 42 1, that the hosting provider's

1 The exemptions from liability established in this Directive cover only cases where the activity of the information society service provider is limited to the technical process of operating and giving access to a communication network over which information mad e available by third parties is transmitted or temporarily stored, for the sole purpose of making the transmission more efficient; this activity is of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature, which implies that the information society service provid er has neither knowledge of nor control over the information which is transmitted or stored.

services must be of a "mere technical, automatic and passive nature" and the provider must be neutral in relation to the content hosted.2 In Google France, the CJEU held: "In order for the storage by a referencing service provider to come within the scope of Article 14 of Directive 2000/31, it is further necessary that the conduct of that service provider should be limited to that of an 'intermediary service provider' within the meaning intended by the legislature in the context of Section 4 of that directive. In that regard, it follows from recital 42 in the preamble to Directive 2000/31 that the exemptions from liability established in that directive cover only cases in which the activity of the information society service provider is 'of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature', which implies that that service provider 'has neither knowledge of nor control o ver the information which is transmitted or stored'."3 In eBay, the CJEU held: "[T]he mere fact that the operator of an online marketplace store offers for sale on its server, sets the terms of its service, is remunerated for that service and provides gen eral information to its customers cannot have the effect of denying it the exemptions from liability provided for by Directive 2000/31 (see, by analogy, Google France and Google, paragraph 116). Where, by contrast, the operator has provided assistance whic h entails, in particular, optimizing the presentation of the offers for sale in question or promoting those offers, it must be considered not to have taken a neutral position between the customer-seller concerned and potential buyers but to have played an active role of such a kind as to give it knowledge of, or control over, the data relating to those offers for sale. It cannot then rely, in the case of those data, on the exemption from liability referred to in Article 14(1) of Directive 2000/31."4 Finally, in this regard, a German case concerning YouTube is instructive. The Hamburg Court of Appeal confirmed that YouTube does not fall under Article 14 ECD, as YouTube (i) gives individualized music recommendations to users and (ii) suggests next to the view ed videos further (presumably) interesting videos.5 Furthermore, YouTube plays an active role, such as to fall outside of Article 14, by its provision of extensive user-friendly functions, such as search, categories with genres, filtering, marking, playli sts, playing functions, recommendations to third parties etc.6 Recital 42 and the CJEU case law is clear and essential in defining the boundaries of Articles 12-15 ECD. Critics have argued that the distinction is obsolete because it was conceived a several years ago, disregarding the further clarifications that practice has brought. The reality is that any attempt at defining business ecosystems is likely to become obsolete very quickly, thus creating legal uncertainty and therefore requiring additional case law to clarify the situation.

Current liability rules do not disincentivize voluntary action by hosting providers Certain services argue that the existing liability regime disincentiv izes them from proactively removing illegal, unlawful, harmful and /or other undesirable content. It is, however, important to recall why this argument is wholly misplaced: It could only have possible application in the case of passive platforms, i.e. intermediary online services that qualify for the liability privileges in the ECD. It is not a consideration for active platforms which, in any case, are not eligible for the liability privileges. In any event, a certain level of activity in addressing illegal content is already required as a condition of the liability privileges, as the CJEU has held that the hosting defense will be unavailable where the service provider is aware of facts or circumstances on the basis of which a diligent economic operator should have identified the illegality in question and acted to remove or disable access to the relevant information. 7 Also, in the Youtube/Uploaded referral to the CJEU, the German Federal Supreme Court (BGH) indicated that taking (proactive) action against illegal content is a factor leading to less liability for the platform, not more.8 We note, also, that in its Communication on Tackling Illegal Content 9 and Recommendation on measures to effectively tackle illegal content online, 10 the Commission sets out its view that taking voluntary proactive measures does not automatically lead to a loss of the benefit of the safe harbor.11 The CJEU has made it abundantly clear that the active role leading to the loss of the liability privilege is linked to promoting illegal content - not to disabling it, which in any event is currently an obligation once awareness or knowledge is obtained. The two cases - Google France and eBay - where the active/passive distinction is confirmed both concerned the question of promotion of 'content' for commercial gain (the "content" in question related to trademark). The cases did not concern removal of content, nor has the CJEU ruled that taking an active role in addressing unlawful or illegal content leads to a loss of Article 14 liability exemption. We are also not aware of any national jurisprudence in this regard. The claim that there exists a need to remove "disincentives for voluntary actions to address illegal content" is further undermined by the fact that such arguments are usually made by active platforms, rather than by the passive platforms that are covered by the liability privileges in the first place. In practice, the notion that there is some epidemic of service providers being penalized for doing the right thing lacks any sufficient factual basis. In our extensive experience fighting illegal content, the MPA is not aware of any cases where platforms we re subject to greater liability on the basis that they were active in removing unlawful and illegal content. Nor are we aware of any evidence base to support the claim that that the current liability regime has in any way hindered the growth of platforms or their ability to provide services to their users. This point was recognized by the Commission in its Communication on Tackling Illegal Content Online: "Specifically in respect of Article 14 of the E-Commerce Directive, in the case L'Oréal v eBay, the Court of Justice clarified that "the mere fact that [an online platform] stores offers for sale on its server, sets the terms of its service, is remunerated for that service and provides general information to its customers cannot have the effect of denying i t the exemptions from liability provided for by [Article 14 of the E-Commerce Directive]". However, there is such an effect, the

Court ruled, "[w]here, by contrast, the [online platform] has provided assistance which entail, in particular optimizing the presentation of the offers for sale in question or promoting those offers". This suggests that the mere fact that an online platform takes certain measures relating to the provision of its services in a general manner does not necessarily mean that it plays an active role in respect of the individual content items it stores and that the online platform cannot benefit from the liability exemption for that reason. In the view of the Commission, such measures can; and indeed should, also include proactive measur es to detect and remove illegal content online, particularly where those measures are taken as part of the application of the terms of services of the online platform. This will be in line with the balance between the different interests at stake which the ECommerce Directive seeks to achieve. Indeed, it recalls that it is in the interest of all parties involved to adopt and implement rapid and reliable procedures for removing and disabling access to illegal information. Although that Directive precludes on line platforms from being obliged to engage in general active fact-finding, it also acknowledges the importance of voluntary measures."12 Europe is a recognized leader in shaping policy at global level, and specifically in regulating online liability. We encourage the EU to continue along this path, marked by the active/passive distinction as interpreted by the CJEU. The European solution is a sound one and should remain in place.

2. "Know your business customer" (KYBC) obligations: a real, tangible, c omplementary solution to Article 5 ECD for all illegal and harmful content with minimal burdens on legitimate businesses Requiring commercial entities to reveal their true identity on the internet would automatically reduce illegal or harmful content online and would greatly facilitate consumers' and business customers' efforts to seek redress. The obligation actually already exists: Article 5 ECD establishes that service providers shall render easily, directly and permanently accessible to the recipients o f the service and competent authorities, identity information, including the name of the service provider, the geographic address at which the service provider is established, the details of the service provider, including their electronic mail address, wh ich allow them to be contacted rapidly and communicated with in a direct and effective manner. The problem is that commercial entities that intentionally distribute illegal and harmful content obviously choose not to comply with this obligation. Under existing law, they face no consequences for failing to do so. Operators of scam websites seeking to defraud consumers, as well as operators of online services illegally distributing gambling, pornography, and other harmful content freely serve EU consumers, using EU-based infrastructure, with an impunity borne of complete anonymity. KYBC case study: Openload The MPA has extensive experience using the tools available under EU law to attempt to trace the operators of illegal services. A high-profile example is Openload, a notorious pirate service that was listed on the Commission's piracy and counterfeiting watch list.

12 Communication, page 11 (footnotes omitted).

After a multi-year, resource-intensive investigation by MPA, this service was revealed to be hosted in and operated from the European Union itself, with infrastructure from EU service providers. When the MPA obtained a court order (pursuant to Article 8 of the Enforcement Directive as implemented by the relevant Member State) directing the EU hosting provider to identify its customer for Openl oad and two other pirate services, we hit a dead end: The listed customer was a defunct shell entity, and the hosting provider admitted that, despite having collected more than €19M in hosting fees: "The data communicated by our client are purely declarative. [Host] therefore does not possess any element permitting verification of authenticity." Thus, the promise of transparent online businesses in the ECD fails in practice because (1) illegal operators do not voluntarily say who they are; (2) the people who sell them the tools to operate their illegal businesses simply don't know who they are and are not incentivi sed to care; and, (3) both sides are presented with very little risk for non-compliance. The DSA can and should close this loophole in EU law. KYBC obligations are an ideal tool to give Article 5 ECD greater effect KYBC obligations impose minimal on no burdens on legitimate businesses, all of which are easily identifiable. Making a defined set of intermediaries responsible for collecting data to confirm the identity of entities with whom they are directly contracting and who need their services to perform their online business activities covered by Article 5 ECD - and verifying that data - should be easy to implement as part of the sign-up process and subsequent periodic re-verifications. In the event the intermediary fails to verify the identity of its commercial customer, it will have to stop providing the services to the respective customer, which would provide an important disincentive against illegal or harmful activity. The company's identity can be easily verified on the basis of an extract from the respective commercial or company register or from a comparable official register, or by submission of the company's founding documents or comparable evidential documents. Categories of intermediaries to be covered by KYBC obligations When considering the categories of intermediaries to be covered by KYBC obligations, it is necessary to find the right balance, recognizing that the problem of illicit operators extends far beyond online marketplace, and often manifests itself through dedicated sites and services distributing scams or illegal content. Against this background, we propose that KYBC obligations should be applicable not ju st to marketplaces, but to the full range of services that enable the possibility of operating an information society service covered by Article 5 ECD. These would include, for example, business applications of hosting and CDN services, payment services, domain name services, advertising services, and proxy services. Sanctions KYBC obligations do not affect the liability privileges in Articles 12-15 ECD, but create new and direct obligations on certain categories of intermediaries. Dissuasive financial penalties should be introduced for non-compliance.

3. Access to WHOIS data as necessary for the public interest Background: What is WHOIS? The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) is the organization which, through its multi-stakeholder community, sets and enforces policies to ensure the secure and stable operation of the Internet domain name system, including the regis tration of domain names. Under the rules and by contract with ICANN, entities known as registries and registrars sell and administer domain names. Amongst other things, registrars and registries are required to collect, share and process certain data from people and companies which register domain names (who they are, how they can be contacted, etc.). This information is commonly referred to as WHOIS data. Until the entry into force of the GDPR in May 2018, these WHOIS data were publicly accessible through a system called WHOIS and used for a variety of purposes, including by law enforcement agencies, private sector organizations and consumers.13 For example, anti-counterfeiting and anti-piracy right holders and groups used WHOIS data to help identify, contact and/or take legal action against registrants of Internet domains where illicit activity, such as trade mark or copyright infringement, was taking place. Other organizations similarly used this data to fight a wide range of online harms, including serious crimes such as fraud, cyber threats (e.g. phishing), fake pharmaceutical products, and child exploitation. Even the inaccurate or outdated in formation contained in WHOIS directories served as a key indicator allowing investigators to link together entire networks of bad actors. There is simply no question that the use of WHOIS data had many benefits for the protection of the public interest and the secure and stable operation of the Internet. Effect of Misguided Application of the GDPR on WHOIS In May 2018, ICANN adopted a temporary policy14 intended to comply with the GDPR. This policy required that the relevant registrar or registry redact most of the WHOIS data, including contact information, from public WHOIS directories. In addition, the temporary policy gave the relevant registrar or registry the authority to decide whether to accept or reject each access request to non-public redacted WHOIS data and required that they grant access to entities that have a legitimate purpose for such access. In practice, almost all access requests (well over 90% in the practical experience of one group) are now denied, even when they conform with the requirements of ICANN's temporary policy. Indeed, even requests that have been made by European Data Protection Authorities for access to non-public WHOIS data to assist in their investigations of potential privacy violations have been denied by registrars.15 A survey conducted by the Public Service Working Group of the ICANN Governmental Advisory Committee of over 50 law enforcement agencies worldwide detailed how the lack of availability of WHOIS data since ICANN's adoption of the temporary policy has interfer ed with the work with of such agencies. 16 Prior to the temporary policy, only 2% of the agencies reported that WHOIS data did not meet investigative needs. Following implementation of the temporary policy, 67% of the agencies reported that WHOIS data did not

13 Registrants have also always been able to make use of privacy proxy services in order to remove certain of their data from appearing in WHOIS records. 14See: https://www.icann.org/en/system/files/files/gtld-registration-data-temp-spec-17may18-en.pdf 15 As described in the 22 May 2020 letter from ICANN President and CEO to the Chair of the European Data Protection Board: https://www.icann.org/en/system/files/correspondence/marby-to-jelinek-22may20-en.pdf 16 See: https://gac.icann.org/presentations/public/icann63%20pswg.pdf

meet investigative needs. Clearly, the temporary policy adopted with the aim of complying with the GDPR has contributed to a lack of accountability and facilitates the use of domain names for illegal purposes, including the violation of EU citizens' privacy rights due to phishing attacks and other abusive activities. It also contributes to decreased compliance with Article 5 ECD, which, as elaborated on above, affirmatively requires online service providers to make publicly available a set of basic identity and contact information that is very similar to WHOIS data. Development of a New Access Policy In May 2018, simultaneously with implementing the temporary policy, ICANN convened an Expedited Policy Development Process (EPDP) to propose a permanent and GDPR-compliant access policy. The EPDP must decide under what conditions registrars and registries can collect and process data and then who can request and be granted access to non-public WHOIS data, such as: what are legitimate purposes to access this data, who can access it and what restrictions are imposed on its use? While the EPDP is labouring to find compromises on a multitude of issues, it remains deeply divided over some fundamental questions. This division includes whether fighting against copyright and trade mark infringement is a "legitimate purpose" and whether data from legal and natural pe rsons should be treated differently. Furthermore, progress on a workable centralized access model for non-public WHOIS data to serve legitimate interests has been stalled. The GDPR was never intended to cut off access to data for legitimate purposes; the u nintended consequences it has had on the availability of WHOIS data deserve careful scrutiny. This concern over the lack of access to WHOIS data has already been raised by the Commission17 and is echoed in the European Parliament. This is not a problem tha t is inherent to the GDPR itself. Some Member States, which are clearly subject to the GDPR, have determined with respect to WHOIS data for their own country code top-level domains that such data serves public interests so that the WHOIS data, even for nat ural person registrants, must be publicly accessible (including name, address and telephone number).18 We urge that as part of the DSA the Commission declare the public interest nature of WHOIS data for both generic and European country code top-level domains and establish that this data should, as it was for decades prior to May 2018, be publicly accessible.

A targeted approach to notice and action From a regulatory standpoint, the objective considerations involved in removing the vast majority of instances of illegal content that is infringing IP rights (for which establishing the illegal nature is usually very straightforward) are entirely unlike the more subjective, context-dependent considerations that are routinely involved in taking down other types of illegal content, including terrorist content, hate speech, etc. So far, the Commission ha s rightfully adopted a "per problem approach" when problems do arise in relation to notice and action, and we believe that this approach has been nuanced and appropriate:

1. Copyright content

In the copyright context, Article 17 of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive creates a notice and action procedure for copyright protected content on certain digital services, whereby a "sufficiently substantiated notice" is required, a complaint mechanism is introduced and the complaint should be pr ocessed without undue delay and subject to human review. No further action is required in the context of copyright content covered by Article 17. This provision embodies obligations concerning prevention and stay-down that apply to OSCCPs who wish to avoid liability for copyright infringement.

2. Harmful content

The Platform to Business Regulation 19 introduced procedural rules regarding the adjudication of harmful content. Platforms must provide a "statement of reasons" before or when taking action against t heir business users. In addition, they must establish an internal complaint-handling system, allowing for appeals. The system must be easily accessible and free of charge while being based on the principles of transparency and equal treatment. Platforms ar e obliged to duly consider, process swiftly and adequately address complaints. The outcome is to be "communicated in an individualized manner". For complaints that cannot be resolved, the platform must provide for an independent mediation process.

3. Terrorist content

The proposal for a Regulation preventing the dissemination of terrorist content online introduced a template for removal orders that the competent authorities shall have the power to issue requiring hosting service providers to remove terrori st content or disable access to it. The template includes a statement of reasons, a URL and where necessary additional information allowing the identification of the content as well as information about the redress available to both the hosting provider an d the content provider. It also requires hosting providers to set up effective and accessible mechanisms for content providers and to promptly examine every complaint that they receive. 1. The existing ECD liability privilege framework remains relevant and useful

The Commission rightfully identifies that there is today a wider spectrum of digital services than in 2000. These services, which intermediate content and whose activity is not of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature, include social media platforms, media-sharing platforms and search engines. These services have indeed been able to grow and flourish in Europe also thanks to the existing legislative framework. The concerns which have arisen typically relate to questions that should be treated in a manner that departs from the ECD, and that are often linked to services that are systemic in nature. But the arrival of new services does not diminish the continuing relevance of Articles 12 to 15 ECD. The activities of these new services are completely distinct from the services dealt with in Articles 12 to 15, and there is no reason to regulate them in the framework of the liability privileges in that instrument. Articles 12 to 15 cover p assive services, such as internet access providers and website infrastructure providers.

Articles 12 to 15 cover p assive services, such as internet access providers and website infrastructure providers. Such services remain the backbone of the internet and play the most essential role in getting digital services to the end user. No digital service can be provided without internet access ("mere conduit" covered by Article 12 ECD), website infrastructure ("hosting providers" covered by Articl e 14 ECD), and improved content delivery through "caching" (covered by Article 13). Importantly, the ECD does not establish liability for digital services but instead only creates liability privileges for these limited digital services, and under very specific conditions. • The ECD is explicit in Recital 42 that these exemptions from liability cover only cases where the activity of the information society service provider is limited to activity which i s of a mere technical, automatic and passive nature. Limiting the liability of newer, non-passive services such as social media and media-sharing in the framework of a revised ECD would defeat the purpose of the DSA: It would diminish rather than enhance incentives to behave responsibly for powerful services. Many of these newer services have long tried to muddy the waters by claiming that they are "hosting providers" in the sense of Article 14 ECD and should therefore be conditionally exempted from liability. The same services advocate today for "clarifying" the scope of Article 14 (by ab olishing the distinction between active and passive platforms) and for introducing broader liability shields. "Know your business customer" (KYBC) obligations: a real, tangible, c omplementary solution to Article 5 ECD for all illegal and harmful content with minimal burdens on legitimate businesses Requiring commercial entities to reveal their true identity on the internet would automatically reduce illegal or harmful content online and would greatly facilitate consumers' and business customers' efforts to seek redress. The obligation actually already exists: Article 5 ECD establishes that service providers shall render easily, directly and permanently accessible to the recipients o f the service and competent authorities, identity information, including the name of the service provider, the geographic address at which the service provider is established, the details of the service provider, including their electronic mail address, wh ich allow them to be contacted rapidly and communicated with in a direct and effective manner. The problem is that commercial entities that intentionally distribute illegal and harmful content obviously choose not to comply with this obligation. Under existing law, they face no consequences for failing to do so. Operators of scam websites seeking to defraud consumers, as well as operators of online services illegally distributing gambling, pornography, and other harmful content freely serve EU consumers, using EU-based infrastructure, with an impunity borne of complete anonymity. The DSA can and should close this loophole in EU law. KYBC obligations are an ideal tool to give Article 5 ECD greater effect KYBC obligations impose minimal on no burdens on legitimate businesses, all of which are easily identifiable. Making a defined set of intermediaries responsible for collecting data to confirm the identity of entities with whom they are directly contracting and who need their services to perform their online business activities covered by Article 5 ECD - and verifying that data - should be easy to implement as part of the sign-up process and subsequent periodic re-verifications. In the event the intermediary fails to verify the identity of its commercial customer, it will have to stop providing the services to the respective customer, which would provide an important disincentive against illegal or harmful activity. The company's identity can be easily verified on the basis of an extract from the respective commercial or company register or from a comparable official register, or by submission of the company's founding documents or comparable evidential documents.
