Etsy, the global two-sided marketplace for unique and creative goods, welcomes the European Commission's announced plans to propose new and revised rules to deepen the Internal Market for Digital Services.

We find it reasonable and appropriate for the Commission to define and enforce the responsibilities and obligations of digital services and online platforms, as long as they are properly informed by the lived experience of platforms like ours, benefit our seller community, while recognising the speed with which technology, risks, threats and solutions shift, and are proportionate to a platform's size and operational capabilities.

In response to the policy options presented to be impact-assessed, we'd like to highlight a couple of key considerations:

Regulating online platforms' procedural obligations

- We encourage the establishment of a harmonised and legally enforceable notice-and action mechanism based on a set of clear procedural obligations. However, any such system must preserve platforms' discretion with regard to user flags. While user flags can be appropriate inputs to platform moderation procedures, they can also often be inaccurate and subject to abuse. User flags should therefore not be considered legitimate notice, for the purpose of quick removal of content.
- Any notice-and-action system will function most efficiently if the experts most capable of identifying illegal content are clearly identified and verified for platforms. We therefore welcome increased effective cooperation with relevant competent authorities and 'trusted flaggers'.
- Procedural obligations must include effective redress mechanisms, such as simple counter notice procedures, to prevent potential abuse, bullying, and over-censorship of legitimate content.

The role of marketplaces and the businesses we represent in ensuring product safety

- The vast majority of Etsy sellers are businesses of one working out of their homes. As microbusinesses, they struggle with the resources to learn about and manage complex compliance obligations. Any obligation arising from the DSA should be designed with these small businesses in mind. Enabling Etsy sellers, including those established outside the EU, to comply with EU legislation in a simplified manner will help these small businesses grow, support their local economies, and offer greater choice to European consumers.
- Responsibilities on marketplaces to ensure product safety should correspond with operational capabilities of their business models. As a third party marketplace, everything Etsy knows about an item is from information supplied by our sellers via product descriptions, tags and images. Our insight into transactions is largely provided via third parties (buyers, sellers, payment processors, shipping carriers, etc.).
- We're supportive of a possible 'know your customer' obligation to verify the identity of our sellers, as this principle would contribute further to ensuring integrity and trust in our marketplace. However, any new measures must be privacy-friendly, proportionate and supported by the right infrastructure in order to be scalable, while enabling the small and microbusinesses we represent to thrive.

Transparency and reporting obligations

- We believe that publicly reporting on our enforcement efforts builds trust in our marketplace and demonstrates our commitment to transparency and accountability. This is reflected in our annual Transparency Report.
- While transparency around outcomes and actions is incredibly useful, we would caution against encouraging public transparency of enforcement methods, as bad actors iterate their own action in response to enforcement efforts, and guarding these strategies improves their effectiveness.

Please find attached our position paper providing greater insight into the considerations mentioned above, and about the inner workings of smaller and mid-sized platforms like Etsy.

Protecting safety, innovation, and free

expression online

JUNE 2020

Introduction

Etsy is the global marketplace for unique and creative goods. It's home to over 65M items, from

handcrafted pieces to vintage treasures. We connect millions of buyers and sellers from nearly

every country in the world. Our mission is to keep commerce human, and we're committed to

using the power of business to strengthen communities and empower people.

Etsy has long functioned as a pathway to entrepreneurship by creating opportunities for people

who might not have started a business otherwise. Our marketplace provides a platform to

enable a global community of 2.8 million sellers-83% of whom are women-to market and sell

their goods to buyers around the world. The majority of our sellers (53%) sold their goods for

the first time on Etsy. Most of our sellers are businesses of one working out of their homes,

often in rural communities. For 32% of Etsy sellers, their creative business is their sole

occupation. For the rest, it provides an important source of supplemental income. Our sellers

pursue their passions, work for themselves, and define success on their own terms. Yet despite

their small size, their economic impact is considerable. Together Etsy sellers sold €4.5 billion in

goods in 2019 alone. For more on our seller community, please see our

2019 Global Seller

Census.

As a third party marketplace, Etsy's primary function is to connect buyers and sellers and to

facilitate trusted transactions. We do not hold physical inventory or manage fulfillment.

Everything Etsy knows about an item is supplied by our sellers via product descriptions, tags

and images. Our insight into transactions is largely provided via third parties (buyers, sellers,

payment processors, shipping carriers, etc.). Sellers may only list items in one of our three

product categories: handmade items, vintage items, and craft supplies.

As of March 31, 2020.

As of March 31, 2020.

2019 Global Seller Census

0.8927 Euros on 31 December 2019. Figure consolidated to include the Etsy and Reverb marketplaces.

Our House Rules define what may or may not be sold on Etsy, including our

Handmade Policy,

Prohibited Items Policy

and

Intellectual Property Policy, among others. Our Trust And Safety

team enforces these policies through several strategies, including notice and action, automated

tools, community flags, and human review. We publish data on these efforts through our

annual

Transparency Report.

The growing role of online marketplaces for the European

economy and society

Platforms like Etsy make it easier for Europeans to start microbusinesses and access the global

market. Creative entrepreneurs on Etsy sold € 4,5 billion in goods in 2019, contributing to

economic growth and creative expression in local communities across Europe. However, as

online platforms have increased in size and become increasingly global, they have not only

created new economic and creative opportunities, but - like many intermediary platforms -

sometimes provided a new venue for the dissemination of illegal and harmful content and

goods. As these ecosystems have become more complex, it is increasingly clear that all parties

must collaborate to ensure safety online. However, any upcoming legislative proposal should

also acknowledge the differences between online platforms across the full spectrum, i.e. a

Content Delivery Network (CDN), Social Network, and Online Marketplace, for example.

Establishing a balanced policy framework for online intermediaries is key to ensuring the

internet remains a forum to promote innovation, creative expression and commerce. In this

respect, policies that protect intermediaries from liability for third-party content are crucial, as we

explain in the first part of this paper. We nonetheless recognise that marketplaces like Etsy

share some responsibility over the safety of our environment, and should take reasonable and

proportionate steps to minimise harm.

As policymakers wrestle with these difficult questions, we believe they may benefit from greater

insight into the inner workings of platforms, particularly smaller and mid-sized platforms like

Etsy, and therefore summarise below many of the proactive measures we use to ensure content

complies with our policies, and maintain the integrity and safety of our site. Specifically, we wish

to share strategies that work well in combating illegal goods and content, while cautioning

against other approaches, given our experience. In view of the potential revision of the EU's

e-Commerce Directive, we hope to see our set of recommendations reflected in an

As of December 31, 2019 ($5b USD). Euro calculation based on the exchange rate of $1 US Dollar to

0.8927

Euros on 31 December 2019. Figure consolidated to include the Etsy and Reverb marketplaces.

evidence-based approach to policy making, and look forward to cooperating closely with

policymakers on new proposals.

Intermediary liability protections enable innovation and expression

Intermediary liability protections enable platforms like Etsy to operate at scale and offer

opportunities to entrepreneurs around the globe. Without such protections, Etsy would be forced

to screen every item before allowing it on our site, a resource-intensive activity that would be

nearly impossible to automate in many circumstances, given the diversity of products, shops

and seller locations on Etsy. As a reminder, most of the +65M items for sale on Etsy are

handmade or vintage items, not mass market goods. Moving to a curated business model would

necessarily curtail the opportunities we currently provide to over two million microbusinesses,

most of whom are women. For example, systematically reviewing handmade products that Etsy

does not possess or control would not be feasible in a global context. Additional liabilities would

also reduce our ability to offer services in multiple markets, undermining the goals of the Digital

Single Market. Finally, liability protections are especially important for startup platforms and

smaller platforms like Etsy, who rely on them to start, grow and compete with larger actors.

Curated, pre-screening models may unfairly favor large actors that have resources and

technologies not available to smaller and startup platforms.

Intermediary liability protections also play an important role in preventing censorship online. If

platforms were liable for every piece of user-generated content, they would be strongly

incentivised to err on the side of caution and block more content than less, likely preventing

legitimate, legal items from being sold. Just as we do not want platforms to incubate and enable

the spread of illegal content, nor do we want them to be subject to inconsistent rules that swing

with political leadership, become the tools of overzealous censorship of unpopular opinions, or

outright repression.

Intermediary liability protections enable marketplaces to take proactive action to keep

their users safe

Intermediary liability protections allow platforms to take concrete action to remove harmful or

illegal user-generated content. They incentivise platforms to take proactive action by holding

them responsible for removing illegal content when they learn of it, and also by giving platforms

the legal certainty that if they do remove content they deem harmful or potentially illegal, they

will not incur new liabilities as a result.

As such, intermediary liability protections allow platforms to go above and beyond the notice

and action regime to proactively identify and remove illegal and harmful content, removing some

of the burden of detection facing rights holders and law enforcement. Ultimately, this allows

platforms to develop new strategies to get ahead and stay ahead of the bad actors, potentially

addressing new threats before lawmakers or enforcement agencies can take action. For this

reason, intermediary liability protections should form the cornerstone of any regulatory effort to

increase safety online.

Intermediary liability protections appropriately distribute responsibility for preserving

safety online among stakeholders.

Every party in the online ecosystem, including platforms, users, law enforcement, and third

parties, hold some portion of responsibility for fostering safety online. When considering updates

to these laws, we encourage policymakers to preserve an appropriate balance of

responsibilities. First and foremost, users must hold primary responsibility for complying with the

laws that govern their actions and products. Etsy sellers must ensure that their products and

business practices meet relevant safety and consumer protection standards, and that they

comply with local laws. If their products or actions do not conform with the law, they may be held

accountable by the appropriate law enforcement agency in the appropriate venue.

However, small businesses also need support in complying with EU legislation. The vast

majority of Etsy sellers are businesses of one working out of their homes. As microbusinesses,

Etsy sellers face unique challenges that often differ from even a ten-or twenty-person small

business. Microbusinesses in particular struggle with the resources to learn about and manage

complex compliance obligations. Time is an entrepreneur's most scarce and valuable resource,

as they must manage every task related to their business operations. For roughly every hour an

Etsy seller spends making or designing her products, she spends another hour on all the other

aspects of managing her shop. We therefore call for the upcoming Digital Services Act (DSA) to

provide consumers and economic operators, especially micro, small and medium-sized

enterprises, with legal certainty and transparency. The Etsy community fully supports efforts to

ensure that consumer protections function in the global marketplace. However, any obligation

arising from the DSA should be designed with these small businesses in mind.

Enabling Etsy

sellers to comply with EU legislation in a simplified manner-with clearly defined obligations and

definitions of illegal content as well as educational resources tailored to their unique

circumstances-will help these small businesses grow, support their local economies, and offer

greater choice to European consumers.

Platforms, on the other hand, must take responsibility for creating a safe and trusted

environment for transactions to occur. They must ensure the elements of the transaction they

control comport with local laws (for example if they process payments or handle distribution).

They must set and enforce their policies to promote safety and security, and must collaborate

with law enforcement and third parties to prevent or stop the spread of illegal activity. To the

2019 Global Seller Census

extent that platforms can partner with law enforcement to promote safety online, they should do

so, but platforms should not become de facto law enforcement themselves, which would be an

inappropriate shift of power and responsibility from government to private businesses.

As a third party marketplace, Etsy's primary function is to connect buyers and sellers and to

facilitate trusted transactions.

Unlike first party marketplaces, we do not hold physical inventory

or manage fulfillment. We are heavily reliant on information outside of our direct physical control

in the detection of unsafe products, and therefore collaborate closely with market surveillance

authorities and trusted third parties to prevent or stop the spread of illegal activity on our

platform.

We therefore request that any new obligations placed upon online marketplace

differentiate requirements between third party and first party marketplaces, based on the very

different knowledge and operational capabilities of these business models.

Similarly, when it comes to a possible 'know your business customer' (KYBC) obligation placed

on marketplaces to verify the identity of our sellers, we believe such a principle could contribute

further to ensuring integrity and trust in our marketplace. However, any new measure in this

direction must be privacy-friendly, proportionate and supported by the right infrastructure in

order to be scalable, while enabling the small and microbusinesses we represent to thrive. Etsy

is committed to working with the relevant authorities to enable and encourage product safety

compliance amongst our sellers. To allow us to effectively check our sellers' identity, any

verification should be done against publicly available databases. Moreover, it's important that

any data collection and verification requirement should be limited to what is reasonably

necessary and proportionate to achieve the intended goals. To reiterate, Etsy sellers tend to be

businesses of one working from their home. The type of data our sellers would have to provide

therefore can be rather sensitive (e.g. home address). Since the process of screening sellers

against publicly available databases for KYBC purposes can be costly and operationally

burdensome, we believe that platforms should be empowered to adopt a risk-based approach to

determine the cadence for rescreening of sellers.

SCOPE: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● While it is increasingly clear that all parties in the online ecosystem must collaborate to

ensure safety online,

the DSA and corresponding obligations will only succeed if they

acknowledge the differences between online platforms across the full spectrum (i.e. a

Content Delivery Network (CDN), Social Network, and Online Marketplace, etc.).

While all such platforms may rightfully be in scope, we welcome targeted sectoral

initiatives that reflect the unique role, risks, and operational capabilities of the different

types of hosting service providers and proportional obligations. In this respect, we

welcome specific rules for online marketplaces in the context of the online sale of

products and services to consumers, but would strongly urge for any such rules and

obligations to further differentiate between third party and first party marketplaces. In a

similar vein, it may be reasonable to exclude marketplaces that facilitate the sale of

goods from legislation that seeks to prevent the dissemination of urgent, high-risk

content, for example viral videos.

● Consider applying requirements that are proportionate to the size, market dominance,

and risk of a particular platform. This approach would mitigate the risk of entrenching

bigger actors and preventing new market entrants. Smaller players will bear the cost of

complying with a complex and burdensome liability rule, and could be discouraged

from even entering the market.

● Any attempt to update the e-Commerce Directive or impose new obligations on

platforms should preserve the prohibition on a general obligation to monitor or filter

content in order to avoid an overbroad impact on lawful content and stifle the

entrepreneurial opportunities platforms create. Moreover, additional clarity on the

protected scope of the filtering prohibition in light of other legislation such as the

Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market, or judicial decisions on filtering for

intellectual property issues that vary by jurisdiction, will help create certainty for

intermediaries and rights holders alike.

Platforms leverage many tools to promote safety online

There are many actions platforms can take to protect users and prevent the spread of harmful

content, especially given the pace of innovation and technological advancement. We find it

reasonable and appropriate for governments to define and enforce those responsibilities, as

long as they are properly informed by the lived experience of platforms like ours, benefit our

seller community, recognize the speed with which technology, risks, threats and solutions shift,

and are proportionate to a platform's size and operational capabilities.

Despite companies' best efforts, it's also important to acknowledge that removing harmful/illegal

content does not remove the views and/or the intent that lies behind those expressions.

Companies can help in identifying harmful content and preventing or slowing its spread, but

technological solutions alone cannot solve these complex societal problems, which demand a

more holistic approach. Further, many of these topics are extremely controversial, with little

consensus regarding what content is harmful and should be removed, as opposed to free

speech that should be protected from censorship. Thus, ever shifting "gray areas" require

difficult decisions that are impossible for a platform to make without reasonable intermediary

liability protections and flexibility in acceptable solutions.

Taking the above considerations into account, any new set of responsibilities that may arise

from an updated e-Commerce Directive must be based on clear, legal definitions and

requirements that platforms of any size can easily implement. Specificity with regard to each

type of harm, definitions, platform responsibilities, and types of platforms implicated will protect

small businesses' ability to comply. As such, any new set of responsibilities must take into

account the operational capabilities, limitations, and challenges of the tools platforms use to

moderate content.

NOTICE AND ACTION

Notice and action provides a reliable and tested horizontal approach to moderate all kinds of

third-party illegal content. Unfortunately, the e-Commerce Directive has not been implemented

consistently across EU Member States, with only some adopting formal notice-and-takedown

systems. We welcome any opportunity to harmonise notice and action rules across the EU. Any

move towards clarifying current notice and action procedures, however, should take into

account the following challenges:

Platforms need clear guidance on what constitutes a valid notice.

While user flags can be

helpful and appropriate inputs to platform moderation procedures, they can also be inaccurate

and subject to abuse. Given the prevalence of competing sellers or speakers on a platform,

those engaging in fraud, and simple mistakes by members of the public, the law must preserve

balance in who can submit a notice and discretion for a platform in accepting a notice. For that

reason, only an officially submitted notice from a competent authority or rights holder should

constitute a valid notice under a Notice and Action regime, especially if that regime includes

time requirements for action. For example, Etsy provides trusted government entities and

organisations with a dedicated email address to identify unlawful listings, which allows us to fast

track takedowns of everything from invasive plants to illegal wildlife trafficking.

Platforms need clear guidance on legitimate notifiers, i.e. who may submit a valid notice.

Platforms, especially small platforms, don't have the in-house expertise to identify all forms of

illegal content in every jurisdiction. For example, startups may not have expertise in determining

the difference between hate speech and free speech in Germany vs. the United Kingdom, or be

able to distinguish a counterfeit good from a legitimate good. In this respect, it's important to

note that the French Constitutional Court recently struck down the 24 hour timeframe of the Avia

law requiring to remove "manifestly illicit '' hateful content. The Court found the requirement

incompatible with freedom of expression since the removal of content could be based on an

user flag, and not a judicial one, and companies don't necessarily have the expertise to make

See, for an example of difficulties even for a large platform,

Prime and Punishment: Directly Dealing in

the $175 Billion Amazon Marketplace

(The Verge, Dec. 19 2018)

such determination. Therefore, we deem that any notice and action system will function most

efficiently if the experts most capable of identifying illegal content are clearly identified and

verified for platforms. For example, as a platform we don't have the expertise to identify

violations of the Indian Arts and Craft Act, but our partners at the Indian Arts and Craft Board

flag violations for our removal. Governments could play a role in identifying and vetting these

third party experts, especially for illegal content not covered by intellectual property laws. This

would give platforms certainty that they are working with appropriate partners for every

jurisdiction and type of illegal content. Further, ensuring diverse platforms partner with the same

"competent authorities" and third party experts would promote consistency of enforcement

across platforms.

Required timelines for action should take into account the capabilities of a small

platform, the risk posed by the type of platform and the riskiness of the content.

It is

reasonable to require platforms to take down the most dangerous content within a specified

period, provided the competent authority is clearly identified in advance, the means by which

they may submit notice clearly agreed upon, and the process established such that it may be

automated (i.e. not subject to human review before taking action, which would require small

platforms to staff moderation support 24 hours a day). However, these requirements should be

tailored to the type of content and platform or business model. For example, the risk of viral

terrorist content is greatest on a social media platform, not a product marketplace. Further, such

extreme measures should be limited to the most risky content, as even automated takedowns

would still need to be reviewed by a human, which is resource intensive, and could be abused

by governments wishing to censor or repress certain types of content.

Counter-notice processes are essential to prevent abuse.

Third party experts and rights

holders are best positioned to identify illegal content, but they can make mistakes or abuse the

notice process to suppress legitimate competition. For example, Etsy sellers may submit take

down requests against other Etsy sellers who do not violate their IP, but compete directly with

their products. In other cases, large rights holders may submit overly broad takedown requests,

demanding legitimate goods be removed from our platform, or submit three notices in rapid

succession in order to get a seller permanently banned before the seller can practically respond.

In those instances, counter-notices are the most effective means an Etsy seller may have to

protect her business.

Rigid "take down and stay down" requirements may harm small creators.

Unfortunately,

we have experienced a substantial increase in false or unauthorised takedowns or IP demands

by non-owners or those attempting to suppress legitimate competition (e.g. cyberbullying,

trolling). We strongly suggest policymakers considering so called "take down and stay down"

requirements ensure platforms retain the ability to weigh contextual information when

determining whether it is appropriate to permanently ban a user, and give users the ability to

appeal a decision. It's appropriate to give violators the chance to resolve violations, and we

want to avoid closing down shops where infringement was likely inadvertent or unintentional, or

where the claim is questionable in merit and legitimacy. In the case of intellectual property, our

sellers are rights holders themselves. Thus, any support given to brand manufacturers to protect

their rights should be built with all the millions of small creators in mind as well. For small rights

holders like the vast array of creative sellers on Etsy, clarity on what constitutes a legitimate

request for takedown are critical for them to effectively protect their rights.

Ensure platforms do not become

de facto

law enforcement or the arbiters of whether

content is or is not illegal.

Platforms, especially small platforms, don't have the in-house

expertise to identify all forms of illegal content in every jurisdiction, and should not rightly

arbitrate legal disputes. Certainly, platforms need to effectively enforce their own policies, but

determinations of legality require detailed legal analysis and should therefore be made by

judicial authorities and law enforcement (as recently emphasised by the French Constitutional

Court in the Avia law). A harmonised notice and action regime allows platforms to combat illegal

content at scale, without inappropriately taking on police or judicial functions.

NOTICE AND ACTION: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Clarify and harmonise notice and actions rules across the EU, to avoid market

fragmentation.

● Establish a dedicated centralised, cross-border portal for verified law enforcement

(competent authorities) to submit a high urgency notice (e.g. when high-risk content is

involved). Community flags should inform and support broader content moderation

efforts, but not constitute valid notice under a notice and action regime.

● Identify and vet legitimate third party experts that platforms may rely on to submit valid

notices.

● Required timelines to takedown illegal content upon receipt of a valid notice is

reasonable, but should be limited to the most high-risk circumstances, and account for

the riskiness of the content and platform.

● Simple counter-notice procedures help combat abuse, bullying, and over-censorship

of legitimate content.

● So-called "notice and stay down" requirements should not be mandated in law, as

platforms need the ability to weigh contextual information to protect users from abuse.

● The individuals responsible for illegal content should be held accountable by law

enforcement and in court. Platforms should not take on inappropriate policing or

judicial functions.

AUTOMATIC FILTERING AND BLOCKING

Technology can be an incredibly effective tool to combat illegal content at scale. Etsy views

preserving our users' safety and marketplace integrity as a core business imperative-and we

have built several tools that aid us in these goals. Our experience building such tools also helps

us understand their limitations. Specifically, there are areas where automated tools cannot

replace human review and moderation. In other circumstances, current technology is not

sufficiently advanced to reliably detect this content. Finally, building effective and scalable tools

requires considerable technology resources and partnerships with experts, which small

platforms may not have sufficient resources to staff. As governments increasingly turn to

technology and automated tools to address the issue of illegal content online, we urge

policymakers to consider the following:

Automated tools still require human review.

For the most part, our automated tools remove

content subject to human review, which means they inform and streamline content moderation

work, but do not completely automate it. Our automated tools may flag high-risk key words to

our moderators, but it's still up to a human to decide whether an item conforms with our policies

or not. Some types of content are extremely context dependent and require nuanced review.

For example, when reviewing listings for hate speech, an Etsy moderator may have to consider

whether the word "queer" is being used as a slur or to reclaim the term. With murderabilia, when

is an item glorifying violence vs. engaging in pop culture fascination with true crime?

Automated tools work best in clear cut situations and depend on clear definitions.

We

have successfully implemented automatic tools for content that is unambiguously illegal. For

example, it is relatively straightforward to automate removal of illegal drugs or weapons. If we

ban a seller, we automatically block new shops from the same device. Any effort to combat

illegal and harmful content should be rooted in clear definitions and requirements, such that

automatic tools can effectively screen for such content.

Best practices for designing automated tools should leverage the experience and

expertise of larger platforms and third-party experts.

When designing automatic tools, Etsy

often consults third party experts, be they specific rights holders or NGOs, to help us

understand the keywords and contextual information most likely to signify illegal content, without

capturing legitimate content. For example, a rights holder can share specific keywords,

categories, price points, and other non-obvious indicia likely to indicate a counterfeit good.

Presumably, other platforms engage in similar efforts, and refine these tools over time as bad

actors find new ways to circumvent them. Government could facilitate a means by which to

share these approaches and best practices among platforms, which would significantly support

small platforms efforts, allowing them to leverage the experience and expertise of larger

platforms. It's worth flagging, however, that such information sharing should not be entirely

transparent, as bad actors are constantly seeking to subvert such efforts, and should not be

able to 'see behind the curtain' of shared enforcement strategies. Reciprocally, given the

limitations of automatic tools, platforms should be given the flexibility to protect users by

accepting counter-notices and denying enforcement of overbroad, inapplicable, or fraudulent

claims that content is unlawful.

Centralised databases and shared resources enable consistent detection and

enforcement across the online ecosystem.

Small platforms may not have the means or

expertise to identify every illegal good or piece of content. However, platforms of all sizes can

leverage technology to compare content on their site with a database of known illegal content,

and automatically remove any matching content. For example, we automatically ban certain

individuals based matches with the Office of Foreign Asset Control (

OFAC

) sanctions list of

individuals. In the same vein, the

Internet Watch Foundation

provides a shared means across

platforms to protect children. Governments, platforms, and third party experts could collaborate

to create and populate such shared tools, enabling smaller platforms to leverage the work of

larger platforms and third party experts, as well as ensuring consistent enforcement across the

online ecosystem. Any such effort should also include effective user rights, recognizing all

systems have errors, and to prevent overextension of such systems.

Some types of content does not lend itself to automated detection.

Etsy hosts over 65M

items, most of which are handmade or vintage goods that do not align with standard product

SKUs, descriptions, or images. Some automatic tools, such as those used to identify

counterfeits, depend on image recognition technology that relies on repeatedly used imagery,

and may not recognize the user photos found on Etsy. Further, machine learning requires large

amounts of data to properly train models. For unique or uncommon violations, it's impossible to

build machine learning models. Machine learning also relies on the past and may be helpful in

matching newly listed items to past patterns, but is not especially useful for spotting emerging

trends or changes in behavior.

Automated tools may capture too much legitimate content.

Efforts to use automated tools

to remove all illegal and harmful content will necessarily result in removing perfectly legal

content. For example, brands may wish for Etsy to automatically remove listings that include

"inspired by X brand" in their description, nominative use, or obvious exceptions to copyright

infringement, where many of these goods would be legitimate. A large number of trademarked

terms also happen to be words in common usage, where a rights holder may nonetheless

demand removal of all listings matching a term. We cannot disregard the real impacts of content

moderation errors on expression and innovation. Taken together, error after error undermines

the trust and legitimacy of legal frameworks meant to protect users, small businesses and rights

holders (including sellers on the Etsy platform), threatening the full benefits of the information

society.

Automated tools are costly to build and maintain.

While automated tools offer significant

promise for content moderation at scale, it is important for policymakers to understand that

developing, implementing, and iterating effective tools requires significant resources and

machine learning capabilities, which may be out of reach for new startups looking to compete

with larger players in the space. Governments should be cautious about forcing these solutions

upon smaller actors, ultimately entrenching the big players' market dominance. For that reason,

we encourage policymakers to align any new proposed requirements with the size and

capabilities of platforms, and to create the means by which technology and tools may be shared

among players in the ecosystem to advance our shared goal of online safety.

AUTOMATIC FILTERING AND BLOCKING: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Look for opportunities to create centralised, verified means to identify illegal content

(list of explosive precursors, verified product photos, etc.)

● Look for opportunities to share information among platforms/open source approaches

(e.g. NCMEC database). However, we have to be careful about how we mandate

transparency of these tools. If we share too much about how our tools work, we risk

giving the bad actors a road map to get around them.

● Look for opportunities to leverage the expertise of civil society groups. Any such

self-regulatory initiatives should, however, include considerations of transparency, due

process and judicial oversight.

● Consider differences across jurisdictions as illegal/harmful content definitions vary by

country, so platforms need to have the ability to block content inside jurisdictions.

● Consider censorship concerns as automated filters could be abused as a tool of

censorship, particularly by repressive regimes.

FLAGGING BY CUSTOMERS AND TRUSTED FLAGGERS

As a platform, we highly value allowing our users to identify and flag content that violates the

law or our House Rules. However, this is not a fail proof system, as it can be a tool used to

attack competition or give power to those who lack specific expertise. Almost all of our user

flags require human review. Per our

2019 Transparency Report

(a high-level recap of our Trust

& Safety efforts over the previous year) 60% of all flags, including machine learning flags and

member flags, were reviewed for accuracy. Improved automated systems generated more alerts

than ever before, causing the increase in flags, and greater capability to automatically resolve

flags led to a decrease in manual review. 77% of flags were reviewed within two working days.

COMMUNITY FLAGS: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Brand manufacturers, law enforcement, civil society organisations should appoint

representatives to be trusted flaggers on platforms, across platforms.

● Escalate flagged content by trusted flaggers for review, and revoke trusted flagger

status if too many decisions/flags are overturned.

● Community/user flags should inform content moderation, but should not be considered

legitimate notice, for the purpose of quick removal of content.

HUMAN REVIEW

Content moderation depends on human review in many, if not most, circumstances. Staffing this

work is one of the greatest challenges facing small and mid-sized platforms, and the reason that

platforms simply cannot review and moderate every piece of content they host. In particular,

human review is essential when: 1) a decision of legality or harmfulness is dependent on

context, 2) definitions of a piece of content are vague/unclear, 3) a legal claim is ambiguous in

scope, especially when the platform has little to no information on the user's content at issue, 4)

disputes between two or more parties need to be reviewed, 5) we need to enforce policies

where we have set the definitions as a matter of internal policy (e.g. our

Handmade Policy

or

Prohibited Items Policy

), or 6) a user appeals or disputes a decision, especially one based on

automated systems.

HUMAN REVIEW: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Human review as a tool is the most difficult to scale, especially for smaller companies.

● Human review is the most difficult solution to establish uniformity of outcome/results

given the natural need of human judgement.

● Consider limiting mandating any such obligation to the highest risk content. It is

proportionate for a company to align higher costs when higher risks are involved.

● Consider alternatives that minimize the scale of human review required (such as

shared databases and tools that leverage the machine learning of larger platforms).

PROACTIVE CONTENT MODERATION & THE IMPORTANCE OF GOOD SAMARITAN

PROTECTIONS

It is important for policymakers to consider strategies to stop the spread of illegal content

separately from those meant to curb harmful content. Any attempt to update the e-Commerce

Directive or add new responsibilities should not extend to harmful content that is not illegal.

When it comes to illegal goods and practices, it is reasonable to place specific requirements on

platforms, provided the supporting definitions and requirements are sufficiently clear and

actionable for platforms of all sizes.

In the absence of clear legal definitions and case law for harmful content, platforms should be

encouraged and supported in their efforts to curb those harms. Yet, we should not face liabilities

and penalties for those proactive efforts. In this respect, Good Samaritan protections are key, as

they give platforms the comfort and security to proactively moderate content, even that which is

not explicitly illegal. For example, per our publicly available

Prohibited Items Policy, we ban

anti-vaccination content and we also prohibit certain medical drug claims based on our values,

such as claims likely to deceive or pose an unreasonable risk to our community.

By rooting our

policies in clearly defined harms and taking proactive measures to enforce them, we can curb

the spread of harmful and misleading content while not crossing the line into censorship of

speech.

Internal policies, such as our

House Rules

Terms of Use

), provide a sensible means by which

companies can proactively limit harmful activities and content that may not be illegal per se.

Enforcing those policies is a legitimate activity for companies to pursue, without crossing the line

into a quasi-law enforcement or judicial functions. Yet developing and drafting clear, fair policies

and enforcement strategies is also resource intensive, particularly when the decisions depend

on significant research and consultation with outside experts. Policymakers should consider

developing and sharing industry best practices on policy creation and enforcement for topics

deemed harmful, but not illegal. For example, Etsy collaborated with other technology

companies and the World Wildlife Fund to

develop and open source policies

that help to curb

illegal wildlife trafficking, which any platform may adopt. This approach could be adopted for

content that is generally agreed to be harmful, but is not strictly illegal.

Finally, platforms have other tools available to stop the spread of harmful content, without

outright banning, removing, or censoring it. Algorithms, particularly in the search functions of

platforms, also constitute a type of proactive measure that can be used to amplify or reduce the

reach and influence of harmful content. In particular, they can be used to make it difficult to find

harmful or illegal content on our site, without outright banning or blocking. For example, Etsy

generally blocks profanity and other harmful content from auto-complete, trending search, and

spell-check. Similarly, a platform may limit access to certain features or functions for harmful

content. Ultimately, this approach prevents the spread of harmful content, while avoiding

censoring speech.

PROACTIVE MEASURES: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Any attempt to update the e-Commerce Directive or add new obligations on platforms

should include a Good Samaritan clause.

● Reasonable sharing of companies' policies and best practices for enforcement should

be shared.

● Governments could help small platforms identify high-risk content or products that are

not explicitly illegal, but tend to incur greater risk of harm, e.g. explosive precursors or

highly regulated products.

OTHER CHALLENGES TO CONSIDER

Enforcement mechanisms:

In efforts to expand enforcement opportunities, several countries

are considering a requirement that platforms appoint a dedicated representative or person who

would be liable for compliance in that jurisdiction. While such proposals may provide a strong

incentive for compliance, they would be nearly impossible for small platforms to operationalize.

The likely impact would be that small platforms facing such requirements would opt not to make

their services available in these jurisdictions at all, further entrenching large players who already

dominate these markets. If every country in the world were to institute such a requirement, we

would significantly diminish the possibility that new players emerge and thrive in the global

online ecosystem.

In a similar vein, we caution against expanding enforcement opportunities to microbusinesses

without a robust support infrastructure in place to help them manage their compliance

obligations. Etsy sellers are eager to offer compliant products, but as businesses of one, they

tend to be very risk-averse. When faced with burdensome requirements (e.g. Article 4 of the

'Goods Package' Compliance and Enforcement Regulation), we believe that most of our sellers

will choose to no longer sell goods into the EU, with the undesirable result of reducing choice for

EU consumers. Further, if countries outside of the EU enact similar requirements, the EU

microbusinesses who sell goods via Etsy would be harmed.

Transparency:

We believe that publicly reporting on our enforcement efforts builds trust in our

marketplace and demonstrates our commitment to transparency and accountability. This is

reflected in our recently released

2019 Transparency Report. Our specialized teams are

dedicated to maintaining the health and integrity of the marketplace by enforcing Etsy's policies,

like our

Seller Policy,

Buyer Policy, and

Intellectual Property Policy. Here are some highlights

from our 2019 policy enforcement:

● We saw a 58% increase in flags for potential

content policy

violations, which we attribute

to improvements in our automated flagging systems.

● We permanently closed 36,420 accounts for content policy violations.

● Breaching our

Handmade Policy, mainly by attempting to resell commercial items, was

the most common policy violation in 2019.

● We had a 16% increase in

intellectual property

takedowns due to increased usage of our

reporting tools by new and existing reporters.

● We rejected almost 16% of intellectual property takedown notices due to insufficient

information, incorrect information, or other noncompliance under Etsy's policies.

● 75% of intellectual property takedowns were executed on accounts located in North

America and Europe.

● We closed 13,906 shops for repeat violations of our intellectual property policies - more

than double the amount of the previous year.

● Despite significant growth in our marketplace, the percentage of orders that resulted in a

dispute remained at 0.3%, consistent with the past three years.

● We handled 17,668 member requests to permanently delete their accounts, more than

double the volume in 2018, due largely to Etsy enhancing privacy controls for all users

and the impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) coming into effect

across the European Union in 2018.

While transparency around outcomes and actions is incredibly useful, we would caution against

encouraging public transparency of enforcement methods, as bad actors iterate their own action

in response to enforcement efforts, and keeping these strategies secret improves their

effectiveness.

Conclusion

Etsy remains committed to building a safer, more trusted marketplace for our sellers and buyers

around the world, and to being a collaborative partner to governments seeking to find pragmatic

solutions to the collective challenges we face. We are hopeful our experiences and suggestions

are useful as policymakers consider these difficult and complex problems, and offer ourselves

up as a resource and partner in developing new solutions to foster a safer internet for all.

For more information, please contact:

Althea Erickson

VP, Global Public Policy and Impact

aerickson@etsy.com

Laura Blanco

EU Public Policy

lblanco@etsy.com

and risk of a particular platform. This approach would mitigate the risk of entrenching

bigger actors and preventing new market entrants. Smaller players will bear the cost of

complying with a complex and burdensome liability rule, and could be discouraged

from even entering the market. ● Any attempt to update the e-Commerce Directive or impose new obligations on

platforms should preserve the prohibition on a general obligation to monitor or filter

content in order to avoid an overbroad impact on lawful content and stifle the

entrepreneurial opportunities platforms create. Moreover, additional clarity on the

protected scope of the filtering prohibition in light of other legislation such as the

Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market, or judicial decisions on filtering for

intellectual property issues that vary by jurisdiction, will help create certainty for

intermediaries and rights holders alike.

Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market, or judicial decisions on filtering for

intellectual property issues that vary by jurisdiction, will help create certainty for

There are many actions platforms can take to protect users and prevent the spread of harmful

content, especially given the pace of innovation and technological advancement. We find it

reasonable and appropriate for governments to define and enforce those responsibilities, as

long as they are properly informed by the lived experience of platforms like ours, benefit our

seller community, recognize the speed with which technology, risks, threats and solutions shift,

and are proportionate to a platform's size and operational capabilities. Despite companies' best efforts, it's also important to acknowledge that removing harmful/illegal

content does not remove the views and/or the intent that lies behind those expressions. Companies can help in identifying harmful content and preventing or slowing its spread, but

technological solutions alone cannot solve these complex societal problems, which demand a

more holistic approach. Further, many of these topics are extremely controversial, with little

consensus regarding what content is harmful and should be removed, as opposed to free

speech that should be protected from censorship. Thus, ever shifting "gray areas" require

difficult decisions that are impossible for a platform to make without reasonable intermediary

liability protections and flexibility in acceptable solutions. Taking the above considerations into account, any new set of responsibilities that may arise

from an updated e-Commerce Directive must be based on clear, legal definitions and

requirements that platforms of any size can easily implement. Specificity with regard to each

type of harm, definitions, platform responsibilities, and types of platforms implicated will protect

small businesses' ability to comply. As such, any new set of responsibilities must take into

account the operational capabilities, limitations, and challenges of the tools platforms use to

moderate content. NOTICE AND ACTION

Notice and action provides a reliable and tested horizontal approach to moderate all kinds of

third-party illegal content. Unfortunately, the e-Commerce Directive has not been implemented

consistently across EU Member States, with only some adopting formal notice-and-takedown

systems. We welcome any opportunity to harmonise notice and action rules across the EU.

consistently across EU Member States, with only some adopting formal notice-and-takedown

systems. We welcome any opportunity to harmonise notice and action rules across the EU. Any

move towards clarifying current notice and action procedures, however, should take into

account the following challenges:

Platforms need clear guidance on what constitutes a valid notice. While user flags can be

helpful and appropriate inputs to platform moderation procedures, they can also be inaccurate

and subject to abuse. Given the prevalence of competing sellers or speakers on a platform,

those engaging in fraud, and simple mistakes by members of the public, the law must preserve

balance in who can submit a notice and discretion for a platform in accepting a notice. For that

reason, only an officially submitted notice from a competent authority or rights holder should

constitute a valid notice under a Notice and Action regime, especially if that regime includes

time requirements for action. For example, Etsy provides trusted government entities and

organisations with a dedicated email address to identify unlawful listings, which allows us to fast

track takedowns of everything from invasive plants to illegal wildlife trafficking. Platforms need clear guidance on legitimate notifiers, i.e. who may submit a valid notice. Platforms, especially small platforms, don't have the in-house expertise to identify all forms of

illegal content in every jurisdiction. For example, startups may not have expertise in determining

the difference between hate speech and free speech in Germany vs. the United Kingdom, or be

able to distinguish a counterfeit good from a legitimate good. In this respect, it's important to

note that the French Constitutional Court recently struck down the 24 hour timeframe of the Avia

law requiring to remove "manifestly illicit '' hateful content. The Court found the requirement

incompatible with freedom of expression since the removal of content could be based on an

user flag, and not a judicial one, and companies don't necessarily have the expertise to make

"competent authorities" and third party experts would promote consistency of enforcement

platform, the risk posed by the type of platform and the riskiness of the content. It is

reasonable to require platforms to take down the most dangerous content within a specified

period, provided the competent authority is clearly identified in advance, the means by which

they may submit notice clearly agreed upon, and the process established such that it may be

automated (i.e. not subject to human review before taking action, which would require small

platforms to staff moderation support 24 hours a day). However, these requirements should be

tailored to the type of content and platform or business model. For example, the risk of viral

terrorist content is greatest on a social media platform, not a product marketplace. Further, such

extreme measures should be limited to the most risky content, as even automated takedowns

would still need to be reviewed by a human, which is resource intensive, and could be abused

by governments wishing to censor or repress certain types of content. Counter-notice processes are essential to prevent abuse. Third party experts and rights

holders are best positioned to identify illegal content, but they can make mistakes or abuse the

notice process to suppress legitimate competition. For example, Etsy sellers may submit take

down requests against other Etsy sellers who do not violate their IP, but compete directly with

their products.

their products. In other cases, large rights holders may submit overly broad takedown requests,

demanding legitimate goods be removed from our platform, or submit three notices in rapid

succession in order to get a seller permanently banned before the seller can practically respond. In those instances, counter-notices are the most effective means an Etsy seller may have to

protect her business. Rigid "take down and stay down" requirements may harm small creators. Unfortunately,

we have experienced a substantial increase in false or unauthorised takedowns or IP demands

by non-owners or those attempting to suppress legitimate competition (e.g. cyberbullying,

trolling). We strongly suggest policymakers considering so called "take down and stay down"

requirements ensure platforms retain the ability to weigh contextual information when

determining whether it is appropriate to permanently ban a user, and give users the ability to

appeal a decision. It's appropriate to give violators the chance to resolve violations, and we

want to avoid closing down shops where infringement was likely inadvertent or unintentional, or

where the claim is questionable in merit and legitimacy. In the case of intellectual property, our

sellers are rights holders themselves. Thus, any support given to brand manufacturers to protect

their rights should be built with all the millions of small creators in mind as well. For small rights

holders like the vast array of creative sellers on Etsy, clarity on what constitutes a legitimate

request for takedown are critical for them to effectively protect their rights. Ensure platforms do not become

de facto

law enforcement or the arbiters of whether

content is or is not illegal. Platforms, especially small platforms, don't have the in-house

expertise to identify all forms of illegal content in every jurisdiction, and should not rightly

arbitrate legal disputes. Certainly, platforms need to effectively enforce their own policies, but

determinations of legality require detailed legal analysis and should therefore be made by

judicial authorities and law enforcement (as recently emphasised by the French Constitutional

Court in the Avia law). A harmonised notice and action regime allows platforms to combat illegal

content at scale, without inappropriately taking on police or judicial functions. NOTICE AND ACTION: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Clarify and harmonise notice and actions rules across the EU, to avoid market

fragmentation.

content at scale, without inappropriately taking on police or judicial functions. NOTICE AND ACTION: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Clarify and harmonise notice and actions rules across the EU, to avoid market

fragmentation. ● Establish a dedicated centralised, cross-border portal for verified law enforcement

(competent authorities) to submit a high urgency notice (e.g. when high-risk content is

involved). Community flags should inform and support broader content moderation

efforts, but not constitute valid notice under a notice and action regime. ● Identify and vet legitimate third party experts that platforms may rely on to submit valid

notices. ● Required timelines to takedown illegal content upon receipt of a valid notice is

reasonable, but should be limited to the most high-risk circumstances, and account for

the riskiness of the content and platform. ● Simple counter-notice procedures help combat abuse, bullying, and over-censorship

of legitimate content. ● So-called "notice and stay down" requirements should not be mandated in law, as

platforms need the ability to weigh contextual information to protect users from abuse. ● The individuals responsible for illegal content should be held accountable by law

enforcement and in court. Platforms should not take on inappropriate policing or

judicial functions. AUTOMATIC FILTERING AND BLOCKING

Technology can be an incredibly effective tool to combat illegal content at scale. Etsy views

preserving our users' safety and marketplace integrity as a core business imperative-and we

have built several tools that aid us in these goals. Our experience building such tools also helps

us understand their limitations. Specifically, there are areas where automated tools cannot

replace human review and moderation. In other circumstances, current technology is not

sufficiently advanced to reliably detect this content. Finally, building effective and scalable tools

requires considerable technology resources and partnerships with experts, which small

platforms may not have sufficient resources to staff. As governments increasingly turn to

technology and automated tools to address the issue of illegal content online, we urge

policymakers to consider the following:

Automated tools still require human review. For the most part, our automated tools remove

content subject to human review, which means they inform and streamline content moderation

work, but do not completely automate it. Our automated tools may flag high-risk key words to

our moderators, but it's still up to a human to decide whether an item conforms with our policies

or not.

Our automated tools may flag high-risk key words to

our moderators, but it's still up to a human to decide whether an item conforms with our policies

or not. Some types of content are extremely context dependent and require nuanced review. For example, when reviewing listings for hate speech, an Etsy moderator may have to consider

whether the word "queer" is being used as a slur or to reclaim the term. With murderabilia, when

is an item glorifying violence vs. engaging in pop culture fascination with true crime? Automated tools work best in clear cut situations and depend on clear definitions. We

have successfully implemented automatic tools for content that is unambiguously illegal. For

example, it is relatively straightforward to automate removal of illegal drugs or weapons. If we

ban a seller, we automatically block new shops from the same device. Any effort to combat

illegal and harmful content should be rooted in clear definitions and requirements, such that

automatic tools can effectively screen for such content. Best practices for designing automated tools should leverage the experience and

expertise of larger platforms and third-party experts. When designing automatic tools, Etsy

often consults third party experts, be they specific rights holders or NGOs, to help us

understand the keywords and contextual information most likely to signify illegal content, without

capturing legitimate content. For example, a rights holder can share specific keywords,

categories, price points, and other non-obvious indicia likely to indicate a counterfeit good. Presumably, other platforms engage in similar efforts, and refine these tools over time as bad

actors find new ways to circumvent them. Government could facilitate a means by which to

share these approaches and best practices among platforms, which would significantly support

small platforms efforts, allowing them to leverage the experience and expertise of larger

platforms. It's worth flagging, however, that such information sharing should not be entirely

transparent, as bad actors are constantly seeking to subvert such efforts, and should not be

able to 'see behind the curtain' of shared enforcement strategies. Reciprocally, given the

limitations of automatic tools, platforms should be given the flexibility to protect users by

accepting counter-notices and denying enforcement of overbroad, inapplicable, or fraudulent

claims that content is unlawful. Centralised databases and shared resources enable consistent detection and

enforcement across the online ecosystem. Small platforms may not have the means or

expertise to identify every illegal good or piece of content.

Centralised databases and shared resources enable consistent detection and

enforcement across the online ecosystem. Small platforms may not have the means or

expertise to identify every illegal good or piece of content. However, platforms of all sizes can

leverage technology to compare content on their site with a database of known illegal content,

and automatically remove any matching content. For example, we automatically ban certain

individuals based matches with the Office of Foreign Asset Control (

OFAC

) sanctions list of

individuals. In the same vein, the

Internet Watch Foundation

provides a shared means across

platforms to protect children. Governments, platforms, and third party experts could collaborate

to create and populate such shared tools, enabling smaller platforms to leverage the work of

larger platforms and third party experts, as well as ensuring consistent enforcement across the

online ecosystem. Any such effort should also include effective user rights, recognizing all

systems have errors, and to prevent overextension of such systems. Some types of content does not lend itself to automated detection. Etsy hosts over 65M

items, most of which are handmade or vintage goods that do not align with standard product

SKUs, descriptions, or images. Some automatic tools, such as those used to identify

counterfeits, depend on image recognition technology that relies on repeatedly used imagery,

and may not recognize the user photos found on Etsy. Further, machine learning requires large

amounts of data to properly train models. For unique or uncommon violations, it's impossible to

build machine learning models. Machine learning also relies on the past and may be helpful in

matching newly listed items to past patterns, but is not especially useful for spotting emerging

trends or changes in behavior. Automated tools may capture too much legitimate content. Efforts to use automated tools

to remove all illegal and harmful content will necessarily result in removing perfectly legal

content. For example, brands may wish for Etsy to automatically remove listings that include

"inspired by X brand" in their description, nominative use, or obvious exceptions to copyright

infringement, where many of these goods would be legitimate. A large number of trademarked

terms also happen to be words in common usage, where a rights holder may nonetheless

demand removal of all listings matching a term. We cannot disregard the real impacts of content

moderation errors on expression and innovation.

A large number of trademarked

terms also happen to be words in common usage, where a rights holder may nonetheless

demand removal of all listings matching a term. We cannot disregard the real impacts of content

moderation errors on expression and innovation. Taken together, error after error undermines

the trust and legitimacy of legal frameworks meant to protect users, small businesses and rights

holders (including sellers on the Etsy platform), threatening the full benefits of the information

society. Automated tools are costly to build and maintain. While automated tools offer significant

promise for content moderation at scale, it is important for policymakers to understand that

developing, implementing, and iterating effective tools requires significant resources and

machine learning capabilities, which may be out of reach for new startups looking to compete

with larger players in the space. Governments should be cautious about forcing these solutions

upon smaller actors, ultimately entrenching the big players' market dominance. For that reason,

we encourage policymakers to align any new proposed requirements with the size and

capabilities of platforms, and to create the means by which technology and tools may be shared

among players in the ecosystem to advance our shared goal of online safety. AUTOMATIC FILTERING AND BLOCKING: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Look for opportunities to create centralised, verified means to identify illegal content

(list of explosive precursors, verified product photos, etc.)

● Look for opportunities to share information among platforms/open source approaches

(e.g. NCMEC database). However, we have to be careful about how we mandate

transparency of these tools. If we share too much about how our tools work, we risk

giving the bad actors a road map to get around them. ● Look for opportunities to leverage the expertise of civil society groups. Any such

self-regulatory initiatives should, however, include considerations of transparency, due

process and judicial oversight. ● Consider differences across jurisdictions as illegal/harmful content definitions vary by

country, so platforms need to have the ability to block content inside jurisdictions. ● Consider censorship concerns as automated filters could be abused as a tool of

censorship, particularly by repressive regimes. FLAGGING BY CUSTOMERS AND TRUSTED FLAGGERS

As a platform, we highly value allowing our users to identify and flag content that violates the

law or our House Rules.

● Consider censorship concerns as automated filters could be abused as a tool of

censorship, particularly by repressive regimes. FLAGGING BY CUSTOMERS AND TRUSTED FLAGGERS

As a platform, we highly value allowing our users to identify and flag content that violates the

law or our House Rules. However, this is not a fail proof system, as it can be a tool used to

attack competition or give power to those who lack specific expertise. Almost all of our user

flags require human review. Per our

2019 Transparency Report

(a high-level recap of our Trust

& Safety efforts over the previous year) 60% of all flags, including machine learning flags and

member flags, were reviewed for accuracy. Improved automated systems generated more alerts

than ever before, causing the increase in flags, and greater capability to automatically resolve

flags led to a decrease in manual review. 77% of flags were reviewed within two working days. COMMUNITY FLAGS: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Brand manufacturers, law enforcement, civil society organisations should appoint

representatives to be trusted flaggers on platforms, across platforms. ● Escalate flagged content by trusted flaggers for review, and revoke trusted flagger

status if too many decisions/flags are overturned. ● Community/user flags should inform content moderation, but should not be considered

legitimate notice, for the purpose of quick removal of content. HUMAN REVIEW

Content moderation depends on human review in many, if not most, circumstances. Staffing this

work is one of the greatest challenges facing small and mid-sized platforms, and the reason that

platforms simply cannot review and moderate every piece of content they host. In particular,

human review is essential when: 1) a decision of legality or harmfulness is dependent on

context, 2) definitions of a piece of content are vague/unclear, 3) a legal claim is ambiguous in

scope, especially when the platform has little to no information on the user's content at issue, 4)

disputes between two or more parties need to be reviewed, 5) we need to enforce policies

where we have set the definitions as a matter of internal policy (e.g. our

Handmade Policy

or

Prohibited Items Policy

), or 6) a user appeals or disputes a decision, especially one based on

automated systems. HUMAN REVIEW: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

● Human review as a tool is the most difficult to scale, especially for smaller companies.
