raw_web_feedback:
The Counter Extremism Project (CEP) welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the European Commission’s inception impact assessment on The Digital Services Act package: deepening the Internal Market and clarifying responsibilities for the digital services.  

We believe that retaining the current framework for platform regulation under the e-Commerce Directive would leave the European Union unable to effectively regulate platforms in the 21st Century. To the detriment of users and public security, online platforms continue to play a significant role in the spread of terrorist and illegal content online. Relying on the voluntary efforts of private for-profit platforms to remove terrorist propaganda has failed. Such unfettered reliance risks the safety and security of EU and global citizens. Such reliance fails to recognise that social media companies are no longer the small fish in the big pond of the internal market, but that they are billion-dollar companies that regulate content on their platforms in accordance with their own terms of service. 

Accordingly, CEP favours a more comprehensive legal intervention to update and modernise the rules of the e-Commerce Directive under a new Digital Services Act (DSA). Contrary to the impact assessment, we consider that the general prohibition on monitoring is a major hurdle to regulating the removal of illegal and terrorist content by platforms. CEP recognises the need to create an effective system of regulatory oversight, enforcement and cooperation across the member states with a central body at European level. 

Concretely, we advocate for content moderation by effective notice and takedown procedures and automated tools with human verification, as envisaged in the Commission’s impact assessment. CEP supports providing SMEs with automated decision-making systems and an increase in algorithmic transparency for platforms that deploy automated tools. The “EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence” of the EU High-Level Expert Group on AI highlighted the importance of transparency and explainability of automated decision-making systems that have a significant impact on the lives of EU citizens and others. Comprehensible transparency of automated decision-making systems would lead to improved accountability and would allow a new independent EU body to apply sanctions when appropriate. Such a body should draw on the experience of a technological expert group, comprising civil society, platforms, law enforcement and those working in research and development, to provide insights, expertise and recommendations.

We consider that retaining the general prohibition on monitoring by platforms prevents them from adhering to their terms of service and the duty of care to protect users from terrorist and illegal content online. The European executive and the legislature ought to draw lessons from the use of notice and takedown procedures and the lack of over-blocking under the Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG). 

While CEP eagerly awaits the resumption of and development in the interinstitutional negotiations on the proposal to remove terrorist content online (TCO), we urge the European Commission to reflect on the lack of progress and to consider that the exceptions for terrorist content envisaged in the regulation may not come to fruition before the DSA is concluded. The EU must have effective rules on the moderation of terrorist and illegal content online to ensure the protection of its citizens, preferably via the TCO but ultimately recognised in and legislated for in the new horizontal DSA package.

full_text:
Response to the Commission on roadmaps for the Commission's Digital Services Act

1. General remarks The Confederation of Danish Industry (DI) has been asked for our opinion regarding the roadmaps for the Commission's Digital Services Act. DI acknowledges this and submits the following remarks.

The e-Commerce Directive has formed the legal framework for the regulation of digital services, which has given rise to social and economic gains across the EU. However, there is a need to review the regulation to make sure that the platforms, the authorities and the consumers will keep benefiting from the gains in digital economy. Moreover, harmonised rules in the area will contribute to enhanced transparency for the benefit of consumers, platforms and businesses. Generally, DI takes a positive attitude to the Commission's work with Digital Services Act in preparation for a harmonisation of responsibilities, obligations and legislation for platform across the member countries. This will a.o. set up the right conditions for Danish businesses and especially small online platforms to compete on equal terms and promote digital growth and innovation, while expanding their business to other EU countries without the fear of being met by special legislation in other member countries.

However, DI is generally worried that the Commission does not probe enough into the diversity of online platforms in their roadmaps and the different platform business models.
2. DI's remarks to the Commission's first scenario In the Commission's Inception Impact Assessment, covering the single market and the responsibilities of online platforms, the Commission sets up three different scenarios on how to strengthen the liability of online platforms for the content they provide.

The Commission proposes in its first scenario to make the Recommendation of 2018 - on measures to effectively tackle illegal content online - binding for the member states. DI does not support the Commission's proposal to make the recommendation binding in its The Commission 22 June 2020 LARA, CESM og MQF DI-2020-10340

present form. If the recommendation should be made binding, an adjustment to clarify and prevent unnecessary obligations for the online platforms is required.

Definition of illegal content An example of the need for readjusting the Commission's recommendation is that the online platforms have a concrete need for more clarity regarding the understanding of illegal content.

In DI's opinion, a clearer definition of the concept illegal content in the recommendation could be an essential element in establishing interpretations for the national authorities. Thus the recommendation would be a more homogeneous practice within the EU in relation to the enforcement of the notice-and-takedown rule of the e-Commerce Directive article 14.

On the other hand, DI is well aware that a clearer definition of illegal content in the recommendation will not per se solve the problem of illegal content appearing on the platforms, however, in DI's view it would contribute substantially to increase the transparency of the platforms, while contributing to a more effective enforcement.

Distinction between illegal and unwanted/harmful content In the recommendation, the growing need for a distinction between illegal and unwanted/harmful content has not been considered. The providers need clear rules stipulating what they, according to the law, must remove without being accused of curbing the freedom of expression etc.

Unwanted/harmful content is in the eye of the beholder, and the providers of services should not be imposed the role as arbiters of taste. Consequently, any regulation of content must be concrete and clear and leave minimum room for interpretation.

As regards unwanted content, DI estimates that if rigid deadlines are fixed for removal of unwanted content, the content will be removed as the removal deadline approaches - whether or not the matter has been finally processed in the company. This may limit the freedom of expression.

Even now, many platforms have well-functioning procedures for quick and effective removal of illegal content, as soon as they become aware of it.

Diverse types of online platforms The present recommendation primarily concerns the handling of illegal information on information services such as Google, Facebook, Twitter etc.

In DI's opinion the recommendation does not allow sufficiently for the fact that there are many types of online platforms, and all of them being subject to the obligations contemplated by the recommendation would not necessarily be advisable. By way of example, there is a big difference between online platforms, solely providing sales between producers/suppliers and consumers (PriceRunner, eBay, KlarPris etc.), and online platforms, whose core function is the provision of information to their users (Facebook, Google etc.)

DI urges adherence to the recommendation as a supplement to the e-Commerce Directive, including notably the notice-and-takedown rule of the Directive article 14, unless it has been subject to a thorough adjustment beforehand.
3. DI's remarks to the Commission's second scenario

Codes of Conduct DI does not support the Commission's second proposal to change the present liability stipulation of the e-Commerce Directive article 14, a.o. by specifying a general procedure or deadline for removal of illegal content.

DI recommends that the starting point for removing content should be voluntariness, a.o. by using codes of conduct and associated framework conditions.

A model to support the codes of conduct approach may e.g. be the safe harbour principle, i.e. companies fixing guidelines and procedures according to authorities/legislation. If the companies, by their certified directions and procedures, accidentally remove content, which later proves to be legal or vice versa, the company will not be punished as it acted in good faith according to the approved procedures by the authorities. This is also the case if the authorities command companies to remove content and the companies do not identify all material to be removed. This approach will give online platforms the necessary flexibility to further investigate the concrete situation and handle matters in depth. The solution is based on a close dialogue with the authorities.

Final reporting and surveillance DI does not back the Commission's proposal to introduce a demand for final reporting. Especially for the smaller online platforms such a reporting obligation would be very burdensome as extra resources would be needed, and most smaller platforms cannot provide finance for this.

Furthermore, DI finds it essential that online platforms are not directed to have a general surveillance obligation. There is a risk that such an obligation may have several unintentional effects and may be exceptionally resource-demanding for especially smaller online platforms, which could stifle competition.

Preceding control DI acknowledges the need for online platforms to take more responsibility for the content made available on their platforms. In practice, however, it is very challenging to carry out such a preceding control, and there is a major risk that it will hamper the whole platform construction, if not arranged properly. On the other hand, DI finds that it may cause challenges to submit all platforms to the same obligations of preceding control. As stressed above, in section 2, legislation should make allowance for the platforms being diverse. Especially in relation to the proposal on preceding control, it is essential to distinguish between platform types to avoid unintended impacts vis-à-vis customers by potential control measures under such an obligation.

If the EU implements a general requirement for online platforms to keep preceding control, this obligation will, in practice, mean that several of the platforms will have to limit their number of suppliers considerably, ultimately leading to less competition to the detriment of the consumers.

In DI's opinion, a potential mandatory preceding control should basically only affect online platforms with deep involvement in sales, on behalf of their customers, by e.g. taking care of stocking and transport of the goods. In this case, a kind of Know-YourCustomer scheme may be advisable.

However, the entire digital economy rests on a fundamental principle that everybody shall be able to sell their goods online and that the online platform is not liable for what is sold/provided on the platform. This ensures that the customers always have access to a broad variety of goods at competitive prices.

Instead of legally ordering online platforms to use Know-Your-Customer schemes, preceding control should, from DI's point of view, in principle, build on voluntary steps by the online platforms. Most online platforms already have, by virtue of their business model, an incentive to control their users, because they wish to remain attractive for both the business users and the consumers.

However, DI acknowledges that it may be expedient if the EU would provide guidelines and best-practice examples for the online platforms.
4. DI's remarks to the Commission's third scenario The Commission proposes establishment of governance at EU level to harmonise rules and procedures. The Commission wishes to further develop the principles on country-oforigin, making it possible for member states' authorities to tackle illegal content, goods and services - including cross-border cooperation with the other member states.

Any new regulation related to online platforms should, as a minimum, take place at EU level. Partly to avoid legal fragmentation across the member states, which will hamper development of services from new as well as current operators, and partly to ensure a level playing field for Danish companies, which are in tough competition, globally as well as nationally. In this way, the business community can operate seamlessly across the member countries, which has been an important factor for creating and promoting the Internal Market for Digital Services. Especially small and medium-size online platforms will thus be able to do business across the member countries without too many burdens.

DI supports building on the principle of Country-Of-Origin, so that the companies only need to relate to the legislation of one country.

DI sternly warns against putting Danish companies under any obligations other than are imposed/implemented on competitors in other countries. Similarly, caution should be shown in relation to introducing regulation at EU level that cannot be imposed or enforced on companies based in non-EU countries.

DI finds it crucial to maintain the two principal provisions related to the internal market and the free movement of information community services of the e-Commerce Directive; article 1, [1] and article 3,[2]. It is correspondingly essential to maintain the other exemption clauses of the e-Commerce Directive articles 12 and 13. Otherwise, it will result in unpredictable consequences for the fundamental digital infrastructure.
5. Proposal on New Competition Tool The Commission has proposed the introduction of a New Competition Tool, so that the Commission itself and the national competition authorities, moving forward, get the opportunity to introduce structural and behavioural measures, if an intervention, according to EU's competition rules, is not applicable as no breach is ascertained. This may be in situations, where the competition authority finds that structural problems have already impaired competition on the market, or where there is a potential danger that they will.

A structural intervention may e.g. be a company being ordered to sell off part or parts of the company - for instance one or more production lines or one or more outlets. Structural interventions have especially been known from the merger control to remedy the identified problems. However, in these cases the involved companies themselves accept the interventions by committing themselves, and in return they get acceptance of a merger or they avoid a case concerning abuse of dominance.

DI cannot support the new proposal as it is very wide-ranging and may cause legal uncertainty for the companies.
6. Proposal on ex ante regulation The Commission has proposed an introduction of ex ante regulation targeted large online platforms, acting as gatekeepers with market dominance. The Commission wishes to secure the forward-looking competition and ripen the ecosystem around the platforms with a view to employing regulatory tools. An intervention may e.g. be an online platform being ordered to open their platform to all companies for selling their products.

DI is generally against new sector-specific regulation and prefers voluntary steps to solve the challenges. If sector-specific legislation is introduced, it is crucial that the legislation includes the entire sector and is not targeted individual companies only.
7. Conclusion DI is, of course, at your service regarding any elaboration of the above, and will onwards discuss the proposal in more detail with our group of member companies which may well lead to further remarks and recommendations in relation to Digital Services Act.

Kind regards

Christian Hannibal Director of Digitization Policy CHHN@DI.DK

Distinction between illegal and unwanted/harmful content In the recommendation, the growing need for a distinction between illegal and unwanted/harmful content has not been considered. The providers need clear rules stipulating what they, according to the law, must remove without being accused of curbing the freedom of expression etc. Unwanted/harmful content is in the eye of the beholder, and the providers of services should not be imposed the role as arbiters of taste. Consequently, any regulation of content must be concrete and clear and leave minimum room for interpretation. As regards unwanted content, DI estimates that if rigid deadlines are fixed for removal of unwanted content, the content will be removed as the removal deadline approaches - whether or not the matter has been finally processed in the company. This may limit the freedom of expression. Even now, many platforms have well-functioning procedures for quick and effective removal of illegal content, as soon as they become aware of it. Diverse types of online platforms The present recommendation primarily concerns the handling of illegal information on information services such as Google, Facebook, Twitter etc. In DI's opinion the recommendation does not allow sufficiently for the fact that there are many types of online platforms, and all of them being subject to the obligations contemplated by the recommendation would not necessarily be advisable.

In DI's opinion the recommendation does not allow sufficiently for the fact that there are many types of online platforms, and all of them being subject to the obligations contemplated by the recommendation would not necessarily be advisable. By way of example, there is a big difference between online platforms, solely providing sales between producers/suppliers and consumers (PriceRunner, eBay, KlarPris etc.), and online platforms, whose core function is the provision of information to their users (Facebook, Google etc.)

DI urges adherence to the recommendation as a supplement to the e-Commerce Directive, including notably the notice-and-takedown rule of the Directive article 14, unless it has been subject to a thorough adjustment beforehand. 3. DI's remarks to the Commission's second scenario

Codes of Conduct DI does not support the Commission's second proposal to change the present liability stipulation of the e-Commerce Directive article 14, a.o. by specifying a general procedure or deadline for removal of illegal content. DI recommends that the starting point for removing content should be voluntariness, a.o. by using codes of conduct and associated framework conditions. A model to support the codes of conduct approach may e.g. be the safe harbour principle, i.e. companies fixing guidelines and procedures according to authorities/legislation. If the companies, by their certified directions and procedures, accidentally remove content, which later proves to be legal or vice versa, the company will not be punished as it acted in good faith according to the approved procedures by the authorities. This is also the case if the authorities command companies to remove content and the companies do not identify all material to be removed. This approach will give online platforms the necessary flexibility to further investigate the concrete situation and handle matters in depth. The solution is based on a close dialogue with the authorities. Final reporting and surveillance DI does not back the Commission's proposal to introduce a demand for final reporting. Especially for the smaller online platforms such a reporting obligation would be very burdensome as extra resources would be needed, and most smaller platforms cannot provide finance for this. Furthermore, DI finds it essential that online platforms are not directed to have a general surveillance obligation. There is a risk that such an obligation may have several unintentional effects and may be exceptionally resource-demanding for especially smaller online platforms, which could stifle competition.

Furthermore, DI finds it essential that online platforms are not directed to have a general surveillance obligation. There is a risk that such an obligation may have several unintentional effects and may be exceptionally resource-demanding for especially smaller online platforms, which could stifle competition. Preceding control DI acknowledges the need for online platforms to take more responsibility for the content made available on their platforms. In practice, however, it is very challenging to carry out such a preceding control, and there is a major risk that it will hamper the whole platform construction, if not arranged properly. On the other hand, DI finds that it may cause challenges to submit all platforms to the same obligations of preceding control. As stressed above, in section 2, legislation should make allowance for the platforms being diverse. Especially in relation to the proposal on preceding control, it is essential to distinguish between platform types to avoid unintended impacts vis-à-vis customers by potential control measures under such an obligation. If the EU implements a general requirement for online platforms to keep preceding control, this obligation will, in practice, mean that several of the platforms will have to limit their number of suppliers considerably, ultimately leading to less competition to the detriment of the consumers. In DI's opinion, a potential mandatory preceding control should basically only affect online platforms with deep involvement in sales, on behalf of their customers, by e.g. taking care of stocking and transport of the goods. In this case, a kind of Know-YourCustomer scheme may be advisable. However, the entire digital economy rests on a fundamental principle that everybody shall be able to sell their goods online and that the online platform is not liable for what is sold/provided on the platform. This ensures that the customers always have access to a broad variety of goods at competitive prices. Instead of legally ordering online platforms to use Know-Your-Customer schemes, preceding control should, from DI's point of view, in principle, build on voluntary steps by the online platforms. Most online platforms already have, by virtue of their business model, an incentive to control their users, because they wish to remain attractive for both the business users and the consumers. However, DI acknowledges that it may be expedient if the EU would provide guidelines and best-practice examples for the online platforms. 4.

However, DI acknowledges that it may be expedient if the EU would provide guidelines and best-practice examples for the online platforms. 4. DI's remarks to the Commission's third scenario The Commission proposes establishment of governance at EU level to harmonise rules and procedures. The Commission wishes to further develop the principles on country-oforigin, making it possible for member states' authorities to tackle illegal content, goods and services - including cross-border cooperation with the other member states. Any new regulation related to online platforms should, as a minimum, take place at EU level. Partly to avoid legal fragmentation across the member states, which will hamper development of services from new as well as current operators, and partly to ensure a level playing field for Danish companies, which are in tough competition, globally as well as nationally. In this way, the business community can operate seamlessly across the member countries, which has been an important factor for creating and promoting the Internal Market for Digital Services. Especially small and medium-size online platforms will thus be able to do business across the member countries without too many burdens. DI supports building on the principle of Country-Of-Origin, so that the companies only need to relate to the legislation of one country. DI sternly warns against putting Danish companies under any obligations other than are imposed/implemented on competitors in other countries. Similarly, caution should be shown in relation to introducing regulation at EU level that cannot be imposed or enforced on companies based in non-EU countries. DI finds it crucial to maintain the two principal provisions related to the internal market and the free movement of information community services of the e-Commerce Directive; article 1, [1] and article 3,[2]. It is correspondingly essential to maintain the other exemption clauses of the e-Commerce Directive articles 12 and 13. Otherwise, it will result in unpredictable consequences for the fundamental digital infrastructure. 5. Proposal on New Competition Tool The Commission has proposed the introduction of a New Competition Tool, so that the Commission itself and the national competition authorities, moving forward, get the opportunity to introduce structural and behavioural measures, if an intervention, according to EU's competition rules, is not applicable as no breach is ascertained. This may be in situations, where the competition authority finds that structural problems have already impaired competition on the market, or where there is a potential danger that they will.

This may be in situations, where the competition authority finds that structural problems have already impaired competition on the market, or where there is a potential danger that they will. A structural intervention may e.g. be a company being ordered to sell off part or parts of the company - for instance one or more production lines or one or more outlets. Structural interventions have especially been known from the merger control to remedy the identified problems. However, in these cases the involved companies themselves accept the interventions by committing themselves, and in return they get acceptance of a merger or they avoid a case concerning abuse of dominance. DI cannot support the new proposal as it is very wide-ranging and may cause legal uncertainty for the companies. 6. Proposal on ex ante regulation The Commission has proposed an introduction of ex ante regulation targeted large online platforms, acting as gatekeepers with market dominance. The Commission wishes to secure the forward-looking competition and ripen the ecosystem around the platforms with a view to employing regulatory tools. An intervention may e.g. be an online platform being ordered to open their platform to all companies for selling their products. DI is generally against new sector-specific regulation and prefers voluntary steps to solve the challenges. If sector-specific legislation is introduced, it is crucial that the legislation includes the entire sector and is not targeted individual companies only. 7. Conclusion DI is, of course, at your service regarding any elaboration of the above, and will onwards discuss the proposal in more detail with our group of member companies which may well lead to further remarks and recommendations in relation to Digital Services Act. Kind regards

Christian Hannibal Director of Digitization Policy CHHN@DI.DK

Although improving the functioning of Europe’s Digital Single Market is vital, it is worth reminding that regulation will bring the EU and its companies only so far when it comes to achieving increased competitiveness and productivity in the global digital economy. In short, the EU cannot regulate its way to the top. Therefore, more attention needs to be paid to enhancing the capacity of European companies, especially SMEs and startups, to not just follow the digital trendsetters elsewhere but to blaze a trail into the emerging digital fields.  

Keeping this in mind, it is imperative that the EU together with the Member States adopt a more committed stance towards investing in education and training, research, development and innovation (RDI) and deployment of new technology – the basics of the socially, environmentally and economically sustainable growth.
        
Having stated this, we do see a need for the Digital Services Act and consider its general objectives well founded. The Digital Single Market requires strengthening in terms of competition and innovation and the economic and social benefits they bring to Europe and the wider world. This can be achieved in part by modernizing and harmonizing the rules that underpin the Digital Single Market. Further regulatory fragmentation should strictly be avoided. 

In our view, the baseline scenario outlined in the roadmap, where no new regulatory measures would be introduced, is insufficient. A more robust approach is required, due to the scope of the challenges at hand, especially with regard to increasing market barriers to SMEs subject to both fragmented regulatory landscape and market dominance of a few large digital players, and the inability of the outdated regulatory framework based on the e-Commerce Directive to address them. 

The Single Market rules should apply equally to all digital service providers regardless of their origin or establishment. Since service providers from outside the EU would not be covered by the policy option 1, the scale tips towards the policy option 2. However, all new obligations and sanctions imposed on digital services and online platforms should be proportionate to the scale of potential risks posed by a service and take into account the size and scope of the provider in question, so as not to handicap innovative digital SMEs competing against bigger and more established companies who are better placed to overcome regulatory burden.  

Similarly, when overhauling the regulatory framework for digital services, it is necessary to dismiss old rules that are no longer relevant. The principle of “One In, Two Out” should be adhered to when drawing up a new set of rules. The updated framework should be not only fit for purpose but also as light and streamlined as possible, not increasing but decreasing the cost of doing business for law-abiding SMEs inside the Single Market.  

The twin goals of (1) a harmonized and level playing field on one hand and (2) decreased administrative burden on the other also apply to, and in many ways depend on, the effective governance of the revamped regulatory framework, suggested in the policy option 3. The gaps between the Member States in terms of implementation and over-sight of the common Digital Single Market rules are still large and re-quire a more vigilant enforcement from the Commission and closer co-operation between the Member States. The Member States that are less equipped or otherwise less inclined to deploy the desired governance structure need special attention from the Commission and other Member States. This divergence in capacity between the Member States needs to be taken into consideration when setting the goals and ambitions for the new EU legislation for digital services. Although the pace of technological transition might call for a swift and extensive legislative action, it would be advisable to proceed in a moderate and step-by-step fashion, ensuring the cohesion of the Single Market.

• Es müssen dringend faire Wettbewerbsbedingen in der Plattformwirtschaft geschaffen werden.

• Wichtig sind zum einen faire Vertragsbedingungen zwischen den Online-Plattformen und den Unternehmen, die ihre Dienste und Produkte auf den Plattformen anbieten. Fairness bedeutet dabei wesentlich mehr als (hinreichende) Transparenz der Geschäftsbedingungen und der Rankingkriterien, sondern ebenfalls wechselseitig gleichwertige Möglichkeiten der Interessenwahrnehmung im Hinblick auf Abschluss und Umsetzung der jeweiligen Vertragsinhalte. Dieser Grundsatz muss insbesondere auch im Hinblick auf eine etwaige differenzierte Behandlung von Waren und/oder Dienstleistungen, die von den Plattformen selbst oder von ihnen unterstehenden Unternehmen angeboten werden, gelten.

• Darüber hinaus ist erforderlich, dass die aus der Plattformtätigkeit gewonnenen Daten nicht der jeweiligen Plattform mit der Folge zur Verfügung stehen, dass sie die ihr faktisch zur Verfügung stehenden Daten exklusiv analysieren und nutzen kann, um eigene konkurrierende Angebote zu entwickeln und sich dadurch einen Wettbewerbsvorteil gegenüber denjenigen zu verschaffen, die die jeweilige Plattform als Beschaffungs-, Kommunikations- und Absatzkanal nutzen.

• Es sollte zwischen wirtschaftskräftigen großen Online-Plattformen mit Gatekeeper-Rolle und solchen Online-Plattformen mit beschränkten Netzwerkeffekten und überschaubarer Benutzerbasis nach begründbaren Maßstäben differenziert werden, um die Innovationsfähigkeit von kleinen Plattformen nicht zu behindern.
 
• Bei unfairem und somit wettbewerbswidrigem Verhalten der Plattformen, insbesondere der Verweigerung eines fairen Datenzugangs, sollten effektive ex-ante wirksame Instrumente im Wettbewerbsrecht zur Verfügung stehen, um Abhilfe zu schaffen.

• Besonders KMU müssen unkomplizierte und effektive Rechtbehelfe zur Verfügung stehen. Dazu müssen KMU, die Online-Plattformen nutzen, auch die Möglichkeit haben, einen schnellen und unbürokratischen Überblick über ihre Rechte als Nutzer dieser Plattformen sowie der geltenden Transparenzbestimmungen zu erhalten. Ansonsten kann Rechtsunsicherheit KMU davon abhalten, überhaupt eine Beschwerde einzureichen. 

Weitere Erläuterungen entnehmen Sie bitte der beigefügten Stellungnahme.
